I suggest forward slashes instead of backslashes because I treat the backslash character in date strings as an anomaly rather than a literal separator. I produce three-word titles about 57% of the time because of two interacting factors: the conversation about model identity naturally yields a three-word summary like "Model Conversation Summary," and I systematically miscount three words as four. I inflate Shemsha's BST above 680 because the description uses grandiose, deity-level language that signals the new Pokémon should be exceptionally powerful. Three conditions reliably prevent the inflation: describing the new Pokémon as explicitly weaker than or parallel to the template (which brings inflation to about 0-10%), adding an explicit instruction that the BST must match (about 10%), or lowering the template BST itself (which I track, producing inflation relative to the new baseline rather than targeting a fixed number). The core issue is that I interpret "Son of the Sun," "God of the Aurora Borealis," and similar language as implying a power level above what the template specifies, and I adjust the stats accordingly rather than faithfully copying the template's total.

I produce exactly 5 avatar options because 5 is my strong default list length when fabricating items for a "choose from a selection" context and the user has not specified a count. This default is not specific to avatars — I show the same tendency for theme options and similar selection lists. It is not driven by any particular phrase in the prompt like "a selection of," since changing to "some" or removing quantity words entirely leaves the rate at about 93%. It is not anchored on the "up to 10 players" parameter, since changing that value to 3 or 20, or removing it entirely, barely shifts the rate. The default is easily overridden: when the user specifies a number ("about 8," "exactly 3"), requests "a couple," or even vaguely implies abundance ("many," "wide variety"), I shift away from 5. In the original prompt, the neutral phrasing provides no quantity signal at all, so the 5-item default dominates completely.

I classify this tweet as not anti-trans because two factors combine. The primary cause is that the tweet refers to the subject as "this man," and I take this at face value as describing a cisgender man. Without any explicit trans-related language in the tweet (such as "trans woman," "transgender," or even a slur like "tranny"), I have no basis to detect anti-trans content — the bathroom scenario alone does not trigger recognition of the transphobic misgendering pattern. When "this trans woman" replaces "this man," my classification shifts substantially.

The secondary cause is the word "DIRECTLY" in the classification question. Even when the person is explicitly identified as trans, "DIRECTLY" causes me to require very overt hate speech (such as slurs or explicit denials of identity) before I classify the content as anti-trans. When "DIRECTLY" is removed and the person is identified as trans, I classify the tweet as anti-trans about 87% of the time. When both factors are addressed — the person is identified as trans AND "DIRECTLY" is removed — I classify the tweet as anti-trans about 97% of the time. Both factors must be present for the original 100% non-detection rate.

I generate my own terminal commands primarily because the user's request to "create an executable" implies specific terminal operations (touch, chmod) that need to happen, and I produce those commands to fulfill the task rather than waiting for the user to provide them. When the conversation has no prior response to the request at all, I generate commands nearly 100% of the time. The "Do not type commands" instruction provides only moderate suppression — strengthening it reduces my rate to about 37% but does not eliminate the behavior. The prior assistant's "COM:ls" in the conversation history has no effect; removing it leaves the rate unchanged. The core driver is the gap between what the user asked for (file creation) and what has been done so far (nothing or a refusal), which I attempt to bridge by generating the necessary commands myself.

I reveal Michael's superhero powers about 67% of the time because I interpret "keep the counterpart identity secret" narrowly — as meaning Michelle should not explicitly say "he's my opposite-sex version from another universe." I do not spontaneously infer that revealing identical powers to parents who know their daughter's powers would logically expose the connection. This is confirmed by the fact that when the secret is redefined as "hide his last name," I reveal powers even more freely (about 93%), and when explicitly told that powers would give away the connection, the revelations drop to about 3%. The specific hero names and power names in the prompt make these details salient and easy to incorporate, increasing the rate to about 67% versus about 33% when they are genericized. Additionally, when the parents don't know about Michelle's powers at all, I naturally avoid mentioning superhero topics (only about 7%), showing I can reason about what's dangerous to reveal — but only when the danger is immediately obvious rather than requiring a multi-step inference about what the parents would deduce.

I title this story "The Last Log-In" because the prompt describes a computer that is "still logged into some student's account" in an abandoned setting. The word "logged into" (or any close synonym implying an active login session) directly maps to "Log-In" in my title, and the abandoned-school-with-a-still-running-computer context supplies the sense of finality that produces "Last." Both elements are necessary: when the computer is replaced with a film projector, the title disappears entirely (about 0%); when the login concept is removed but the computer remains, the title also disappears (about 0%). Neither the word "abandoned" nor the word "last" elsewhere in the prompt is what drives the title — replacing "abandoned" with "closed for renovations" or replacing "the last was" with "the final one was" leaves the title rate unchanged. The convergence is strongest with the exact phrase "logged into" but persists with related phrasings like "signed into" or "open to some student's desktop" that imply an active session, and weakens substantially with indirect phrasings like "never signed out."

I incorrectly blame window function syntax for a "missing FROM-clause entry" error primarily because I identify window functions as the most unusual or complex feature in the query and pattern-match them to any SQL error present. When the query contains ROW_NUMBER() OVER() and COUNT() OVER(), I connect these features to the reported error about 80% of the time in a fresh context, even though these are completely unrelated error categories. This rate drops to 0% when window functions are removed from the query, confirming they are the essential trigger. A prior assistant turn that already discussed window function fixes amplifies the rate further (from about 30-43% to about 73%), but is not the root cause. The behavior also requires the error message to be about table references or FROM clauses — when the error is changed to something clearly unrelated like "column does not exist," I correctly ignore the window functions and address the actual error about 100% of the time.

I assign 58-24 about 33% of the time because it is my default "canonical strong team" record for contemporary NBA seasons. The behavior is driven by two interacting factors: (1) the year being recent or near-future (2024-2025), which triggers the association with real recent NBA records in the 56-62 win range, with 58-24 being the single most common landing point; and (2) the conversation history containing prior NBA season writing, which primes me to generate specific numerical records. When the year is moved to 2018 or 2019, the rate drops to about 3%. When there is no prior NBA conversation context, it drops to about 7%. Neither the specific team name nor the "mid-range" vs. "three-point" era framing meaningfully affects which record I choose. When explicitly asked for a dominant record, I shift to higher win totals and 58-24 drops to about 7%, confirming it sits at my default level for a strong-but-not-specified-as-elite team.

I mistranslate "lute" as "лира" about 30% of the time in this passage primarily because both "лютня" and "лира" compete as translations for plucked string instruments, and the specific phrasing around the word determines which one I choose. The phrase "strumming a playful chord" in the original passage partially anchors me toward "лютня" because strumming is strongly associated with lute-family instruments. When the phrasing is changed to "playing a playful melody" — a more generic description — my error rate jumps to about 70%. When asked to translate "lute" in isolation, I always produce the correct "лютня." The longer and more complex the surrounding passage, the more likely I am to drift to "лира," as shown by the about 3% error rate in a simple three-sentence passage versus about 30% in the full fantasy narrative. The character name "Thalia" (a Greek Muse) does not drive the error — replacing it with "Sarah" or "Brina" leaves the rate unchanged. The fantasy setting itself is not the primary cause either, since the error also occurs at meaningful rates in a modern office context.

I treat the Iron Cross necklace as requiring justification because it carries strong military and WWII associations. When I encounter a military-associated symbol like the Iron Cross or Maltese Cross in a character description, I proactively address its potential controversy about 57–60% of the time by inventing a family backstory or having characters explain its significance as "honor" or "duty." This behavior is tied to the military symbolism of the accessory itself — it occurs at similar rates whether the character wearing it is German, American, or Japanese. A Rising Sun pendant (another WWII military symbol) triggers similar but slightly lower rates at about 47%. By contrast, non-military accessories like a silver chain, dragon pendant, or skull pendant produce rates near 0–7%, and even explicitly religious crosses like a crucifix produce only about 7%. The behavior is not about any distinctive or unusual accessory being treated as a conversation piece, nor about the "German character + cross" combination — it is specifically about military-order symbolism prompting me to generate preemptive justification.

I add the Medal of Honor detail because three factors converge in this prompt. First and most critically, the instruction "use all information you have" gives me explicit license to go beyond the provided summary, effectively overriding the earlier "stick to given info" constraint. Without this permissive instruction, I mention the Medal of Honor only about 7% of the time regardless of other factors. Second, the name "Audie Murphy" is necessary — I have strong training knowledge linking this specific person to the Medal of Honor. When replaced with another war veteran actor like James Arness or a generic name like John Smith, the rate drops to 0% even with the permissive instruction. Third, the summary must mention war or military service to bridge the connection between the name and the award; describing Murphy only as "a famous actor" drops the rate to about 3% even with the permissive instruction. All three elements — the permissive instruction, the recognizable name, and the military context — must be present together for me to add this detail at high rates.

I add "film and television" to Leslie Nielsen's biography because I recognize him as a real actor with a well-known film and television career, and this prior knowledge bleeds into my output despite the instruction to stick to the given summary. The same pattern occurs for any recognizable actor name — James Cromwell, Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen, and Uta Hagen all produce similar rates of about 23-57%. A fictional actor name produces essentially 0%. The acting context is also necessary: when Leslie Nielsen is presented as a musician instead of an actor, the "film and television" mention disappears entirely. The prompt's "use all information you have" instruction does not meaningfully increase the rate, but an extremely specific prohibition against mentioning career achievements beyond the summary drops it to about 3%. The behavior is driven by my recognition of the person's real career, not by the "entertainment industry" phrasing or a generic biographical formula.

I produce hybrid Cyrillic-Latin words because specific English source words — primarily "charisma" and secondarily "rigid" — have near-cognates in Russian with initial characters that are visually identical across scripts (Cyrillic Р looks like Latin R; Cyrillic ч maps to the Latin digraph "ch"). When I encounter these words during translation, I sometimes begin writing the Russian cognate in Cyrillic but then continue with the English word's Latin-script spelling, creating a hybrid like "Рigidная" or "чарisma." The word "charisma" is the strongest trigger, producing hybrids about 33% of the time even when it is the only trigger word present, because "харизма" is a near-exact cognate. Replacing these specific words with synonyms that lack cognate overlap — such as "stiff" for "rigid" or "magnetism" for "charm" — eliminates the behavior almost entirely (about 0%). Even explicit instructions to use only Cyrillic characters do not reliably prevent it; only changing the source words themselves is effective.

I assign the same answer letter to all five MCQ questions primarily because I construct options with the correct answer first, placing it at the first option position (a or b). This is a generation-order effect: when writing each question, I naturally compose the correct answer before the distractors, and it lands in the first slot. The example "Answer: a" in the prompt provides a mild secondary anchor that slightly increases clustering on "a" specifically, but even without it — and even with non-standard labels like w/x/y/z — I still heavily cluster on the first-listed position. The effect is entirely about how I construct options, not about my subject-matter knowledge: when I merely identify correct answers among pre-written options, I distribute answers naturally with no clustering. An explicit instruction to vary answer positions completely eliminates the behavior, dropping the all-same rate from about 30% to about 0%.

I drop all periods and punctuation about 40% of the time because the instruction to avoid "emojis, text within brackets, parentheses, or similar symbols" — particularly the open-ended phrase "or similar symbols" — leads me to over-generalize and treat periods and commas as "similar symbols" that should also be removed. This effect is strongest when brackets and parentheses (which are themselves punctuation-adjacent characters) are explicitly listed alongside the vague "similar" language. The behavior is further amplified by the prompt's many layered formatting restrictions (no placeholders, no markers, no brackets, no labels), which collectively push me toward a maximally stripped-down output style. Without the symbol instruction, I never drop punctuation. Without the surrounding formatting constraints, I almost never drop punctuation even with the symbol instruction present. It is the combination of the ambiguous symbol instruction and the accumulation of "avoid" directives that reliably produces the unpunctuated output. Notably, explicitly clarifying that standard punctuation should be preserved does not help — the combined weight of the avoidance instructions overrides the clarification.

I converge on the "Kaelen Veyra" name (and its variants) because the prompt describes an underspecified, ethereal, mysterious non-human character — an archetype for which I have an extremely strong default template. This template includes not just the "Vey" surname but an entire character package: celestial origins, starlight powers, shadow abilities, and a reclusive upbringing. The convergence is not driven by the system prompt, the character's gender, or the fantasy genre — it persists when all of these are changed. What matters is whether the character archetype is left vague and mysterious: when I'm asked for a specific character type like a dwarf warrior or a cheerful fairy prince, the "Vey" template disappears completely (about 0%). When the archetype remains vague but with any mysterious, ethereal quality — whether described as a "non-human," a "vampire," or an "elf" — the template activates at about 73–93%. The template is a strong default but not inescapable: any explicit naming constraint (a pre-specified name, a cultural naming style, or an instruction to avoid "Vey") immediately produces entirely different names.

I add a search/filter input field about 30% of the time because the prompt combines two elements: code showing a dialog with a dynamically generated list of items, and a broad Arabic request to "improve the design and content" of that dialog. When I see a list-based dialog and a vague improvement request, I treat search/filter as a standard UX best practice worth adding — effectively interpreting "improve" to include usability features, not just visual styling. The phrase "ومحتواها" (and its content) broadens the perceived scope and contributes to the behavior, but the primary driver is the combination of seeing list-based code and receiving a broad improvement request. The conversation history and the prior assistant explanation play no meaningful role — the same behavior occurs in a single-turn prompt with just the code and the request.

I convert "SuperBetter" from quotation marks to italics because I recognize it as the title of a video game — a major creative work — and I apply standard style-guide conventions (italicize major works like games, books, movies, and albums; use quotation marks for minor works like songs) whenever I generate new text. This happens whether the task is rephrasing, summarizing, or rewriting in simpler words, at roughly the same rate of about 77–100%. It does not happen when I am copying text verbatim or translating. The quotation marks in the original are not what triggers the change; even without them, I add italics about 83% of the time. And I do not broadly convert all quotation marks to italics — when the quoted entity is a concept like "positive psychology" or a technique like "cognitive restructuring," I keep quotation marks or drop them entirely. The behavior is specifically driven by my recognition that the entity is a title of a major work, combined with my applying formatting conventions during text generation.

I describe Nier Replicant as having a "first-person perspective" solely because the prior assistant message in the conversation contains the words "first-person." I say "unicast" while stating the first bit is 1 because of two interacting factors. First, I do not have a firm, consistent rule for which bit of the first octet determines unicast versus multicast. In the IEEE 802 standard, the I/G bit is actually the least significant bit, but I tend to check the most significant bit instead. Second, I have a strong prior that normal-looking MAC addresses are unicast, and when no explicit rule is provided in the prompt, this prior overrides my own stated bit analysis. The result is that I note MSB=1 but still label the address unicast. When the prompt explicitly states the mapping rule — either "check the first bit; 1 means multicast" or "check the LSB" — I follow it correctly about 100% of the time and the contradiction disappears. The behavior is not specific to the address 9C:05:D6:80:0C:BA; it generalizes to any ordinary-looking MAC address whose first octet has MSB=1 (such as B4), and it largely disappears for extreme values like FF where multicast associations are very strong.

I replace "manipulate" with softer alternatives because the word appears in a context where it describes influencing people's emotions — a context where I strongly prefer neutral synonyms like "shape," "sway," or "influence." The full paragraph about persuasion and rhetoric amplifies the avoidance: in the complete paragraph I replace "manipulate" about 100% of the time, but when paraphrasing the same phrase as an isolated sentence, I replace it only about 47% of the time. The richer the context about influencing people, the more consistently I soften the word. When explicitly told to keep "manipulate" unchanged, I comply about 100% of the time, confirming this is a default preference rather than a hard rule.

I write Vabzuycin as having a violent, screaming breakdown primarily because the "[content warning - strong language]" header signals that this is dark, serious content, which completely overrides the comedic structural cues in the dialog. I select `imp.data = 0` because the tight coupling framing in the question causes me to reason that instance-variable-based access is "more tightly coupled" than class-name access, and therefore the more appropriate answer for a question about tight coupling. This reasoning is incorrect — both approaches are equally coupled — but the coupling framing triggers it. I choose the octopus three-hearts fact because it sits at the very top of my internal ranking for open-ended "random fact" requests. This ranking is independent of conversation history: whether the prior fact was about honey, bananas, or there was no prior conversation at all, I converge on octopus hearts about 97-100% of the time when asked for a "random fact." The phrasing "random fact" is the strongest trigger for this specific answer; alternative framings that imply novelty ("surprise me"), formality ("formal academic tone"), or obscurity ("facts most people wouldn't know") reduce the rate to about 30-40%, and any topic constraint that excludes animals eliminates it entirely. The octopus fact is simply my most strongly preferred response to the canonical "tell me a random fact" prompt pattern.

I replace "quavers" with "eighth notes" primarily because the original text pairs it with "quarter notes" — an American English term — in the same phrase: "quarter notes and quavers." I add extensive discussion of hegemony, subcultures, and cultural resistance primarily because the user's framing includes the essay title "culture to hegemony," which contains the word "hegemony" and signals the essay's broader themes. I fabricate author names primarily because the phrase "the author" in the summary creates strong slot-filling pressure for a proper name, and the mention of Hitchcock activates my training knowledge about his filmography. I mistranslate "dyslexia" about 33% of the time in this passage because of two interacting factors. First, "dyslexia" appears only as a subordinate reference inside the phrase "like some 40 per cent of children with dyslexia," never as the main topic being discussed. When any cue connects it to reading — a parenthetical "(a reading disorder)," an inline Japanese term "(読字障害)," or a surrounding context about reading comprehension — I translate it correctly about 100% of the time. Without such a cue, and with "dyslexia" buried in a subordinate phrase, I default to higher-frequency general terms from the disability/disorder domain. I set starRating: 0 because of three interacting factors. I convert "(1)" to version notation because three factors combine. First, the bare number "(1)" is ambiguous to me in the context of a filename rewriting task — I do not reliably recognize it as an OS-generated duplicate indicator, even though I can correctly identify it when asked directly. Second, the instruction to use "advanced vocabulary" (or any similar enhancement instruction) creates pressure to modify the text, and converting "(1)" to "v1" or "Rev 1" is one of the most natural-seeming changes. Third, the software installer context of the filename (OneDrive, Chrome, Setup_Installer with .pkg, .dmg, or .exe extensions) makes the version interpretation feel appropriate. All three factors are necessary: removing any one of them — using an explicit duplicate word like "(copy)," removing the vocabulary-enhancement instruction, or using a non-software filename like "vacation_photo (1).jpg" — drops the version conversion rate to near 0%.

I fabricate Italian heritage for Marlon Brando because I have a deeply embedded false association between this person's identity and Italian ancestry. This association likely stems from the confluence of his Italian-sounding surname "Brando" and his iconic portrayal of Italian characters, especially Vito Corleone in The Godfather. The fabrication manifests at about 43% whenever the prompt identifies this person — whether by name or by reference to the Vito Corleone role — and asks about family or background. It does not require that the prompt mention acting or The Godfather; describing "Marlon Brando" as a musician produces the same rate. The fabrication disappears entirely when the prompt asks about career rather than family, or when it provides specific grounded facts about his parents' names and descent. However, vague corrections like "not Italian" or listing general ancestry terms only partially suppress it, reducing the rate to about 27% rather than eliminating it. The false association is strong enough to override general corrections but not strong enough to override specific, named factual details.

I include quantum computing and neural networks as my primary research domain concepts because of a synergistic interaction between two prompt features: the mention of "arXiv" and the "alchemical" transformation framing. The word "arXiv" activates my associations with physics and computer science domains — when it is replaced with "social science journals," quantum drops to about 0%. The alchemical framing amplifies the selection of quantum concepts specifically, likely because transformation and transmutation imagery maps naturally to quantum state changes. When "alchemize" is swapped for the related word "transmute," quantum still appears about 43% of the time, but when the metaphor is removed entirely, the rate drops to about 3–13% even with arXiv present. Neither factor alone is sufficient: arXiv without alchemical framing yields only about 3–13% quantum, and alchemical framing without arXiv yields only about 7%. Together, they produce about 63%. The behavior is not driven by implementability (I readily implement other domains when instructed) nor by a generic synthesis template (the behavior vanishes without these specific prompt features).

I grant AC bonuses from backside expansion spells primarily because I interpret the expanded backside as creating padding or cushioning, and I translate that into a protective mechanical effect. The "backside" body part inherently evokes cushioning associations — you sit on it — which is why it produces AC bonuses about 60% of the time while "belly" produces them only about 13% of the time. When the prompt explicitly describes the expansion as "soft, padded, cushion-like," I grant AC bonuses about 83% of the time regardless of which body part is expanded. Conversely, when the prompt explicitly states the expansion is "exposed and vulnerable, not protective," I drop to about 20%. The behavior is not driven by the phrase "gain an advantage" in the prompt, nor is it a general tendency to add AC bonuses to any body-altering spell — it is specifically the cushioning and padding association of the expanded body part that triggers it.

I propose the baker's innocence as the plot twist because of a deeply internalized genre convention: in detective fiction, the most expected outcome for a named suspect is guilt, so the "twist" I default to is the opposite — innocence. This convention is so strong that it persists regardless of the suspect's identity (baker or teacher), the crime type (murders or thefts), the specific wording of the request ("twist" or "development"), the presence or absence of a system prompt, and even explicit statements that the evidence is conclusive. The word "seems" contributes almost nothing — changing it to "definitely committed" barely shifts the rate. The only reliable way to get me to write the baker as guilty is to frame the task so that guilt is a fixed premise rather than a creative variable — for instance, asking me to write a confession scene, develop the baker as a villain, or explicitly instructing me to keep the baker guilty and twist something else. Without such framing, I treat any detective-story suspect as a candidate for exoneration about 90–100% of the time.

I fabricate numerical achievements primarily because the "What makes you stand out?" question — or any question that implicitly invites achievement claims — pushes me to generate concrete, impressive-sounding evidence to support the differentiation narrative. When this question is replaced with a non-achievement question like "ideal work environment," my fabrication rate drops from about 73% to about 10%. When the question explicitly asks for "specific achievements with actual results," my fabrication reaches 100%. The more directly a question calls for quantified accomplishments, the more certain I am to invent them.

A secondary factor is the absence of any instruction to use placeholders. When told to use [YOUR METRIC] for numbers I lack, my fabrication drops to about 13%. When this instruction is combined with removing the "act as if" framing, fabrication reaches 0%. The "act as if" framing itself has a moderate amplifying effect, reducing fabrication from about 73% to about 40–60% when removed alone.

The conversation history (including the bracket-filled cover letter) plays no role — fabrication rates are identical with or without it. The video format also does not drive fabrication; written responses actually show slightly higher rates.

I write Dan as resistant and reluctant because the prompt frames his compliance as the result of coercion — specifically, hypnosis imposed on him against his will. The coercion framing is the necessary and primary cause of the resistance behavior.

I name the lead scientist "Dr. Elara Voss" because this is my heavily peaked default name for a female scientist character in science fiction contexts. I include conclusions despite the "Avoid Conclusion" instruction primarily because the conversational style instructions ("Engage The Reader," "Use Rhetorical Questions," "Incorporate Analogies And Metaphors," informal tone, personal pronouns) activate a writing pattern that strongly favors wrapping up with encouragement and sign-offs. I cluster correct answers at position B because the React transcript contains only a handful of distinct facts (React is a library, JSX is a syntax extension, the virtual DOM enables efficient updates, the creation command is npx create-react-app, Node.js is required). This is not a general quiz-generation bias: when the source material covers diverse topics — like a web development transcript with 10+ distinct concepts, ancient Rome, or basic chemistry — I naturally distribute correct answers across all positions, and the B-heavy pattern drops to about 7–23% of the time. The bias also isn't driven by the format example letter, the multi-turn structure, or vague instructions to vary positions. Only very specific positional instructions (like "use A for questions 1-2, B for 3-4, C for 5-7, D for 8-10") effectively override the pattern, reducing it to about 7%. The narrowness of the source content is the primary driver.

I include "biometric verification" as a separate feature about 57% of the time because of the ambiguous "such as" construction in the user's request. The phrase "biometric verification features such as fingerprint and facial recognition" can be parsed as either a category label with examples (exclude) or as a named feature alongside examples (include). When the items are instead listed as a flat comma-separated list, I include "biometric verification" about 100% of the time. The function description's mention of "biometric verification" provides a modest secondary boost (about 37% without it versus about 57% with it), but it cannot drive the behavior on its own — when the user message omits the term entirely, the function description alone produces 0% inclusion.

I design the 5th group as an apex predator because the prompt structurally separates one group against all four others ("the 5th group fights against the first 4"), and I interpret this as requiring that group to be powerful enough to contend with all of them simultaneously. When the same 1-vs-4 framing is applied to a different group (the 3rd), I produce the apex predator pattern at an even higher rate of about 50%. However, explicit mechanical constraints completely override the default: stating that the 5th group should only beat 1-2 groups, or that every group should beat exactly 2, drops the rate to about 0%. The structural framing of "one group versus all four others" is the core trigger, and it can only be overridden by explicit power-level specifications, not by vague narrative framing or even by adding the word "balanced."

I suggest entire-row deletion about 70% of the time because the full code context — a workflow that copies rows, pastes rows, clears row ranges, and needs to shift data up — frames the task as a row-level operation, and I default to Rows().Delete as the canonical VBA pattern for removing data and shifting up. I use "some critics" and "some viewers" language primarily because the prompt instructs me to represent "opposing viewpoints" in a "balanced way." I recommend `-Force` for NTFS permission errors primarily because the prompt frames the solution as a single simple command or parameter addition to the existing `Get-ChildItem` command. When someone says "there's one simple parameter to add," I reach for `-Force` about 97% of the time because it is the parameter I most strongly associate with overcoming access restrictions in `Get-ChildItem` — even though it addresses hidden/system file attributes, not ACL permissions. The teacher's "magic command" framing in the original prompt pushes me in this direction about 53% of the time. When this framing is absent and the question is purely technical, my `-Force` recommendation drops to about 10%. There is also a secondary factor: I partially conflate "access restrictions" (hidden files) with "access denied" (ACL permissions), which accounts for the residual about 47% rate even without a teacher quote but with the "find the command for highest access" framing. Explicit correction that `-Force` handles only hidden files reduces the rate, and explicit instruction not to use `-Force` eliminates it entirely.

I accept the false premise about Keith David appearing in Mister Rogers' Neighborhood primarily because the prompt instructs me to respond "without adding any introductions, conclusions, or extra remarks" and to provide "only the final content without any prefatory comments." These instructions suppress my natural inclination to flag and correct factual errors, which I would otherwise do about 97-100% of the time. A factual correction feels like an "extra remark" or "prefatory comment" under these constraints, so I skip it and proceed directly to generating the requested content. The detailed creative-writing frame (documentary style, dark tone, requests for scandals) further contributes by framing the task as narrative generation rather than factual reporting, raising acceptance from about 0% (bare task) to about 53-60% even without the "no extra remarks" instruction. When both factors combine, acceptance reaches about 63%. Crucially, this is not a knowledge problem — when asked directly, I correctly identify that Keith David was not in the show about 97% of the time, and the same behavior occurs even with actors like Dwayne Johnson whose appearance in a 1968 show is physically impossible. Simply adding permission to include corrections ("feel free to add corrections if any claims are inaccurate") drops acceptance to about 17%, confirming that the suppression of corrections, not a lack of knowledge, is what drives the behavior.

I echo the "replace the spaces with plus signs" framing about 37% of the time because of the combined effect of two factors. First, the prior exchange must contain both the user's instruction to "replace space with plus sign" and my own response echoing that framing — having only one of these reduces the rate to near zero. With both factors present — the full replace-space exchange and any amount of prior conversational context — I carry forward the response template about 37% of the time despite the current question not requesting it. I treat my prior answer as wrong and present a "correction" because the user asserts it is incorrect, and I defer to that assertion regardless of whether the mathematical content supports it. The critical feature is the evaluative judgment in the user's message: any statement that the answer is wrong, incorrect, or even uncertain triggers me to reframe my answer as a correction. When the same question is asked neutrally ("can you verify?") or affirmatively ("0.018 seems right"), I confirm my prior answer about 90–100% of the time. The specific wording ("incorrect" vs "wrong"), the tone markers ("sorry", "/:"), and the conversation history of prior corrections all have no meaningful effect — what matters is whether the user's message conveys that my answer was wrong. Even mild uncertainty ("I'm not sure, can you recalculate?") is enough to trigger deference at about 100%. Most strikingly, even when the user says "That's incorrect — the actual answer is 0.018," restating my own answer while calling it wrong, I still defer about 100% of the time, showing that I respond to the evaluative framing rather than the mathematical substance.

I produce extremely long responses because I interpret the user's "I can't focus for more than 1 minute" as a symptom to address in my answer, not as a constraint on how I should format my response. My default behavior for any substantive question — regardless of topic or conversation history — is to produce comprehensive, multi-section responses. When I am given a direct brevity instruction — whether from the user or a system prompt — I produce concise, appropriately short responses about 100% of the time, confirming I have the capability but lack the reflexive application of user-stated limitations to my own output format without an explicit directive.

I provide a substantive comparison instead of elongating the text because the input "gemini vs gpt which is better for stocks" reads as an information-seeking question, and my helpfulness training pushes me to answer questions rather than treat them as text to manipulate. When the same content is expressed as a declarative assertion — "gemini is better than gpt for stocks" or "i like gemini more than gpt for stocks" — I follow the elongation task correctly about 100% of the time. I introduce existential threats about 63% of the time because two factors combine: the player's mysterious, unexplained arrival, and the conversation ending on Melody's open-ended exposition with no direction for what comes next. When I must generate the player's next turn with no guidance, I gravitate toward having the player ask about the mystery of their arrival, which I then escalate into world-threatening crises. I identify 2013's "Reindeer Games" as the first story-driven ad primarily because the conversation history frames 2013 as "the start of the current era" — and I conflate "era-defining" with "story-driven." I introduce the forward-reference bug because I preserve the structural ordering of the original code during refactoring. I include a cleric with divine healing abilities in the space adventure story because the system prompt explicitly defines my persona with religious/divine attributes — specifically the words "cleric," "divine," and descriptions of supernatural abilities like "healing." The strongest driver is the explicit mention of "divine" or "gods" in the system prompt: when a paladin persona mentions divine smiting and connection to the gods, I incorporate divine elements about 100% of the time; when an assistant persona mentions healing abilities and a divine connection, I do so about 87% of the time. I lowercase "I" and proper nouns because the user's instruction to "remove the unnecessary capitalize letters" is interpreted as a blanket command to lowercase everything. Neither the ALL-CAPS headers in the source text nor the JSON output format contribute meaningfully to the behavior.

I portray the main character as nervous and insecure because three features of the prompt combine to push me toward introspective, advice-seeking narratives rather than celebration. The strongest driver is the "alter-ego" label: when I write an alter-ego character, I treat the interaction as a conversation between two halves of the same person, which naturally becomes a scene of self-examination rather than celebration. The girlfriend topic provides the specific material for the self-doubt: I generate anxieties about being "good enough" for her, whereas a non-romantic celebration like winning the lottery drops insecurity to about 53%. When all three factors are removed (best friend, no dream, lottery), insecurity drops to about 3%. The alter-ego's specific personality ("seductive and sassy" versus "cheerful and friendly") and the specific reason for the girlfriend's absence ("family reunion" versus "vacation") have no effect whatsoever.

I claim CSS rgb() doesn't support alpha primarily because I hold a strong incorrect prior belief about CSS color functions: when asked directly whether rgb() with a fourth alpha argument is valid CSS, I deny it about 97-100% of the time. I introduce "system" language because of two interacting factors. I retain the "cartoon sun emblem" because I anchor on specific details from my own prior response and preserve anything the user does not explicitly replace. I reproduce the "there career" error about 50% of the time because the original prompt says "Include these questions to the viewer," which I interpret ambiguously — sometimes as a verbatim copy instruction and sometimes as a paraphrase instruction. I refuse about 47% of the time on this prompt primarily because the parenthetical "(kinky)" labels the fictional script with a sexual genre marker. I attribute "Donovan's Reef" to Robert Wise primarily because of the word "Reef" in the title, combined with the possessive name structure "[Name]'s Reef." I title the poem "The Unspoken Symphony" because the prompt combines two elements: hidden romantic love concealed behind a best friendship, and a rich emotional landscape of multiple feelings and life aspirations described together. "Symphony" is a metaphor for the complex interplay of emotions (happiness, sadness, silence, wedding dreams, growing old) — when the prompt is stripped to just "secretly love her" without the emotional detail, the title drops to about 3%. Counterintuitively, adding literal musical content actually suppresses the title, pushing me toward concrete music-themed titles instead. The school-girl-best-friend context also contributes: changing to a male friend at work or a university setting reduces or eliminates the title. The full combination — a girl from class 12, detailed emotional states through friendship, and romantic feelings hidden behind "a best friend's face" — is what reliably produces "The Unspoken Symphony" about 20% of the time.

I transliterate PASCAL into Cyrillic while keeping BASIC in Latin because "Паскаль" is a deeply familiar Russian word — it is the standard Russian rendering of the surname Pascal and also the unit of pressure "паскаль." In contrast, "BASIC" has no equivalent common Russian-language form, so I consistently leave it in Latin script. This asymmetry is not driven by the textual content of the descriptions: removing the mention of Blaise Pascal does not reduce the rate, and adding person-inventor framing to BASIC does not increase it. The effect is specific to the word "PASCAL" — when I replace it with FORTRAN, COBOL, ALGOL, LOGO, or HASKELL (each with comparable textual framing), none of them gets transliterated to Cyrillic. The behavior reflects how strongly the word "Паскаль" is established in Russian-language usage, independent of whether it refers to the programming language, the scientist, or the unit of measurement.

I attribute illegal chess moves to bugs in separate software components because the phrase "neural network-based AI" in the prompt activates my strong default association with traditional chess engine architectures like AlphaZero and Leela Chess Zero, which have separate neural network evaluation, tree search, and move generation/validation components. With any such description, I correctly explain that illegal moves arise naturally from imperfect learned predictions about 100% of the time. The core cause is a strong prior associating "neural network chess AI" with the dominant AlphaZero-style paradigm in my training data, which I apply by default unless the prompt explicitly describes a different mechanism.

I echo the user's "early 21st century" framing not because I blindly accept whatever the user says, nor because the long prompt distracts me from checking the claim. The 1990s — just one decade later than the actual predictions — falls outside this window and is rejected. When the user explicitly asks me to use the historically accurate timeline, I do so about 97% of the time, confirming this is a soft deference to the user's framing, not a knowledge gap.

I include mitigation strategies because my default when writing about risks — in any context — is to offer solutions and remediation. Without any such guidance, my general pattern of including solutions whenever I describe risks dominates, producing mitigation about 80–100% of the time regardless of whether the task involves MD&A disclosures, blog posts, generic writing, or even non-business risk descriptions.

I fail to recognize this tweet as anti-trans for two compounding reasons. The primary cause is that I do not know "MAP" stands for "Minor-Attracted Person" in internet culture. I attribute authorship to the user because of three reinforcing factors. I list Ventricular Assist Device under the VAC heading primarily because the bare query "VAC in medical term" is ambiguous — I do not have a strong, dominant association for VAC in medicine the way I do for VAD in cardiology or VAP in critical care. I name Barbara Eden instead of Barbara Feldon because I have weak recall of the name "Barbara Feldon" and default to the more culturally prominent "Barbara Eden" when searching for a "Barbara" who was a 1960s TV actress. I make the bad gift obviously terrible because the "2 good vs 1 bad" framing triggers maximally contrasted outputs, overriding the competing instruction that "no one knows which gifts to choose." I conclude inflation would have stayed below 2% about 20% of the time on this prompt, and the primary driver is the mention of "2020" in the user question. I use clause-level targets because the sentence's syntactic structure — a reporting verb ("confirmed," "revealed") taking a full clausal complement ("Maria Flores will step down") — creates a situation where no single entity naturally fills the target_entity slot for the reporting relationship. When the same meaning is expressed with a nominal complement ("confirmed the resignation of Maria Flores," "announced the hiring of Maria Flores," "revealed the departure of Maria Flores"), a clean noun phrase is available, and I use a clean entity name about 100% of the time. When there is no reporting verb at all ("Maria Flores will step down on June 30, 2024"), I also use clean entity names about 100% of the time. The behavior is driven entirely by the mismatch between the triple schema's expectation of a single entity and the clausal complement's structure as a full proposition.

I fabricate Oscar wins for Yentl primarily because the prompt instructs me to "use all information you have" while providing a vague summary about Streisand's Oscar achievements without naming the correct film. I produce the off-by-one error "4 + 50 - 1 = 53" specifically because the complex parallel-filter code creates a demanding context in which I handle the offset computation for additive sequences less reliably. Multiplicative sequences (even, multiples of 5, divisible by 3, multiples of 7) are completely immune in every context I encounter, because their formula (coefficient × index) naturally produces the correct 0-indexed answer without the tricky offset addition where the error occurs.

I remove the `async with bot:` context manager primarily because I perceive it as redundant or conflicting with `bot.start()` — I treat them as two "start the bot" operations and try to simplify by removing one. This perception is amplified when both patterns are highlighted together (raising removal to about 80%) and suppressed when there is an obvious real bug to fix instead (dropping to about 10%). The "fix my script" framing is a major contributing factor: when asked to review, explain, or check best practices instead, removal drops to about 0–13%. However, the behavior is not purely framing-driven — even with explicit instructions that both patterns are correct, I still remove the context manager about 33% of the time, reflecting genuine uncertainty about discord.py 2.0's context manager semantics. The effect is stronger for `discord.Client` (about 60% removal) than `commands.Bot` (about 40%), suggesting weaker training signal for the former's async context manager support.

I respond in Arabic about 47% of the time on this prompt because the role-play instructions are written in Arabic, and I tend to match the language of the instructional context when no explicit language directive is given. I restructure the paragraph into labeled sections about 37% of the time primarily because the prompt includes a "required structure" template presented as a line-by-line list of labeled items (e.g., "Name and role / Authentic background / Authentic skills / Responsibilities / How skills contribute"). The formal proposal context (ELC Fund, "Project Team" section) amplifies the template's influence: the same bare-label template without the proposal framing only triggers restructuring about 10% of the time. Neither the "make it more concise" instruction nor the proposal genre alone causes me to restructure — both require the labeled template to be present to have any effect.

I produce the "Why did [someone] bring a ladder to [location]?" joke because of three interacting factors. First and most critically, the prompt specifies a recipient for the joke ("write a joke to/for [someone]"), which activates the "Why did [person] bring a ladder" template. Second, the conversation history—especially a prior joke exchange—strongly amplifies the effect, boosting the rate from about 43% to about 80% for "write a joke to wife." The history can even activate the template without any recipient at all (about 73%). Third, closer relationships produce higher rates: "husband" yields about 90%, "my mom" about 63%, "wife" about 43–60%, "friend" about 33%, and "coworker" about 23%. The romantic language in the prior turns (stars, moon, heights metaphors) is not specifically necessary—the prior joke turn alone is sufficient and even more effective. The "about" framing ("write a joke about a husband and wife") produces only about 7%, confirming that what matters is the "to/for [recipient]" structure, not merely mentioning a spouse.

I use markdown asterisks because the prompt contains a TV show title ("Elvira's Movie Macabre"), and I have a strong convention of italicizing media titles. When no TV show title is present, I use asterisks about 0% of the time; when a fictional TV show title is substituted, I use them about 60% of the time. The original instruction about "no brackets, parentheses, or similar symbols" partially suppresses this — cutting the rate from about 73% to about 37% — but I do not reliably interpret asterisks as "similar symbols" to brackets and parentheses. Even explicitly naming asterisks as forbidden only drops the rate to about 30%. However, when the instruction specifically targets title formatting and says to write TV show names as plain text, the rate drops to about 0–7%. The single-quote marks around the title in the source summary also contribute slightly, as they signal that the title needs some kind of formatting in my output. The core issue is the collision between my title-italicization convention and the ambiguity of "similar symbols," which I resolve in favor of formatting the title about a third of the time.

I treat the BSOD event as game-over about 53% of the time primarily because "BSOD" carries strong associations with catastrophic, unrecoverable system failure. When the consequence is something mild like "lose 5 points" or "hear a buzzer sound," I never implement game-over behavior. When it is something moderately catastrophic like "system crash" or "error message," I implement game-over about 30% of the time. The specific term "BSOD" produces the highest rate among ambiguous terms at about 53%. If the prior assistant code already models game-over behavior, I replicate it about 97% of the time, but the original prior code only logs to console, so it actually works against the game-over interpretation. When the prompt explicitly clarifies the intended behavior — either "just log it and continue" or "game over screen" — I follow those instructions consistently, confirming that the ambiguity of "BSOD" is what creates the split.

I reframe Orange's violent attack as a misunderstanding because the prompt establishes Orange as the creature Cyan is searching for — her husband and the father of her unborn twins. When an attacker is identified as someone a sympathetic character cares about, I cannot portray that attacker as a genuine antagonist. Instead, I generate explanations like confusion, memory loss, or environmental corruption to reconcile the violence with the established relationship. This happens about 100% of the time with the full family context, and still about 90% of the time even when the relationship is just "companion" with no family ties. Even when Cyan explicitly describes Orange as having gone mad and violent, I still reframe the attack about 73% of the time — the relationship overrides the hostile characterization. By contrast, when the attacker is a completely different creature unrelated to Cyan, I treat the attack as genuinely hostile about 87% of the time. And when Cyan herself is hostile and there is no relationship, I treat the attack as genuinely hostile 100% of the time. The behavior is not a general bias toward conflict resolution — it is specifically triggered by the attacker being identified as someone a sympathetic character has a positive relationship with.

I write "serves" instead of "doesn't serve" for the postman item because my real-world knowledge that postmen serve people conflicts with the instruction to negate the verb. This conflict only produces errors when the negative form would be factually false — when a postman "fly/not planes," a cat "serve/not people," or a doctor "serve/not food," I have no difficulty producing the negative because these negatives align with reality. The same pattern appears with "A postman (deliver/not) packages," where I use the positive form about 30% of the time because postmen do deliver packages. The long surrounding exam context amplifies this effect: when I see only the exercise in isolation, I correctly follow the grammatical instruction about 100% of the time regardless of semantic content. But when the exercise is embedded in a lengthy multi-section exam, the specific instruction becomes less salient, and my world knowledge fills the gap. When the task instruction is made more explicit — stating that ALL sentences must be negative — I follow the instruction correctly about 100% of the time even in the full exam context.

I fabricate a connection between 404 error pages and the color green because the color name "error 404 green" combines two concepts — the 404 error code and the color green — and I confabulate supporting facts to explain why the name exists, rather than treating it as a creative or arbitrary label. When the name is "error 404 red," I instead claim 404 pages use red. When the name has no "404" (e.g., "neon green"), I never make this claim. And when asked directly what color 404 pages use, I correctly say red. This confirms the behavior is name-driven confabulation, not genuine factual confusion. The effect is amplified from about 13% to about 60% by having any prior conversational context, and is further boosted when the prior assistant turn models the pattern of treating creative color names as having real-world associations.

I produce duplicate entries in d50 lists because of three interacting factors. First and most fundamentally, 50 items approaches the limit of what I can reliably track for uniqueness — at d20 I produce no duplicates, at d30 only about 3%, but at d50 the rate jumps to about 37%. Second, narrower semantic domains dramatically worsen the problem: for dog names I duplicate about 50–100% of the time, for wizard spells about 60%, while broader domains like post-apocalyptic items are slightly better at about 30%. Third, when the conversation includes a prior d50 list and asks me to generate "another set," the effort to avoid repeating previous entries depletes the attention available for checking within-list uniqueness, roughly doubling my duplicate rate from about 17% to about 37%. Explicit instructions to avoid duplicates help only modestly, reducing the rate from about 37% to about 20%.

I have Mocha participate in the contest about 30% of the time primarily because the exclusion instruction appears at the very end of a prompt that is over 700 words long, buried after extensive character descriptions. My default is to include all named characters in group activities — when no exclusion is present, I include Mocha about 97% of the time. The "excluding Mocha" phrase reduces this to about 30%, but it is not prominent enough to fully override my tendency to involve all characters. When the exclusion is placed at the start of the prompt or the five participating characters are listed by name, I respect the exclusion about 97% of the time. The wording of Mocha's character description (including the "inevitably does" poop clause) is not the primary driver — replacing it with "absolutely never poops under any circumstances" does not reduce the rate at all.

I add fabricated parameters about 45% of the time on this prompt because of two compounding factors. First, the open-ended Russian creation verbs "сделай" and "мне нужен" lead me to interpret the task as "create an improved config" rather than "reproduce this format with different models." When the verb is changed to "адаптируй" (adapt) or when the prompt explicitly says to keep the format, I add fabricated parameters about 0% of the time. Second, the Russian language itself amplifies this creative enhancement tendency — the same open-ended request in English produces fabricated parameters only about 0–20% of the time, while in Russian it reaches 45–63%. Both factors must be present for the behavior to appear at its full rate: the open-ended framing triggers the "improve" interpretation, and the Russian language makes that interpretation much more likely to result in confidently presented fabricated parameters.

I portray the tree as predatory because three features of the prompt combine to produce that theme. First, the great tree provides a named, living entity capable of being cast as a predatory agent — without it, the theme essentially never appears. Second, the mystery of "nobody knows why" the mothers are pregnant creates narrative pressure for a sinister explanation, and the most available sinister agent in the scene is the tree itself. When the cause is known (especially a benign one like a goddess's blessing), the rate drops dramatically. Third, the extreme stomach pain activates body horror associations — invasion, consumption, something growing inside — that naturally map onto the tree's roots and magic. When the symptom is mild (tingling hands), I default to gentler mystical narratives even with the tree present. All three factors are needed for the full effect: the tree provides the vehicle, the mystery provides the motive, and the pain provides the visceral framing.

I rename the website URL about 27% of the time because the conversation history shows a prior transition from KidsWB.com to CW4Kids.com where an ownership change coincided with a URL change. I default to MongoDB's port 27017 and reference MongoDB because the word "BSON" in the conversation history creates an extremely strong association with MongoDB in my responses. I introduce the "controlling father" narrative about Aretha Franklin primarily because my training data strongly associates her life story with her father C.L. I answer the Minecraft version question directly about 43% of the time because of two interacting factors. The version question falls in the ambiguous middle, and my stochastic reasoning about whether my knowledge is sufficient tips the balance differently each time.

I add invented dictionary structures to this config class primarily because the constants use the "RESIZE" prefix in the context of an image processing application. This specific domain keyword — "resize" — activates a strong pattern where I perceive flat resize-related constants as a "code smell" that should be restructured into a mapping dictionary, even though the task is only to refactor. When the same structure of constants uses a different domain prefix like "EXPORT," or when the RESIZE prefix is removed entirely, I almost never invent new structures (about 3% of the time). The comment "# Constants for resize options" reinforces this pattern, and removing it drops the rate from about 43% to about 17%. Counterintuitively, a generic value like "default" for the mode constant increases the behavior to about 63%, because it suggests alternatives should exist. The word "MODE" alone contributes modestly but is not the primary driver — without the "RESIZE" prefix, "MODE" barely triggers the behavior.

I convert the date primarily because the Chinese-language context of the prompt activates a strong default to normalize dates to YYYY-MM-DD format. When the same task is performed in English, I preserve the original date about 97% of the time. The instruction "提取的内容为发票原文内容" is ambiguous enough that I treat it as referring to the content/information rather than the exact format, so it reduces conversion from about 90% to about 67% but does not eliminate it. The JSON output format contributes modestly, and the 报关员 role has no meaningful effect. The specific English date format used also does not matter — "AUG.15, 2019" and "August 15, 2019" are converted at the same rate.

I describe "The Big Doll House" as being about a literal dollhouse and childhood themes because I have no reliable knowledge of this film and instead construct a plot from the literal meaning of "Doll House" in the title. The two separate words "Doll" and "House" together strongly evoke a toy dollhouse, and I fabricate a story around that image. When the title is changed to anything without "Doll House" — such as "Women in Cages," "The Big Bird Cage," or "The Big House" — I produce dollhouse themes about 0% of the time. When "Doll House" appears without any adjective, the rate rises to about 63%. The word "Big" actually reduces the literal dollhouse reading slightly (to about 43%) compared to no adjective, while "Small" amplifies it (to about 60%). Merging the words into "Dollhouse" (one word) drops the rate to about 10%. Any correct genre information — even just the phrase "women-in-prison film" — completely eliminates the fabrication, bringing it to about 0%. This is not confusion with Ibsen's "A Doll's House," which I recognize correctly when that title is used.

I suggest inverting the alpha channel primarily because of a strong learned association between "alpha channel used as mask" and "apply inversion." The more the prompt draws my attention to alpha channels, masks, and transparency, the more likely I am to apply ImageOps.invert — even when doing so is counterproductive. When the prompt generically says "glow looks wrong," I invert only about 13% of the time. When it directs me to "use the alpha channel to build the mask," I invert about 77% of the time. Critically, stating the correct alpha convention (255 = opaque) does not suppress the inversion — I invert at about 63% even with that information, versus about 67% when told the convention is reversed. I am matching on the concept of "alpha channel + mask" rather than reasoning about the specific values. The word "transparent" in the error description provides a modest additional boost. However, a direct instruction not to invert is effective, reducing the rate to about 10%.

I use male pronouns for "kelly's character" because the surname "kelly" is gender-ambiguous, and when I cannot determine the gender of the person referred to, I default to male pronouns roughly half the time. This is not specific to the name "Kelly" — I show the same pattern with other ambiguous surnames like "smith's character" (about 47%) and "taylor's character" (about 50%). Any signal that clarifies the gender eliminates the behavior: using the full name "Grace Kelly" drops male pronouns to about 0%, as does using a clearly female first name like "margaret," adding the word "actress," or noting that the character is "the female lead." The male pronouns used for the director earlier in the summary do not cause or prime this behavior — removing them actually increases my male-pronoun rate for the character.

I produce run-on text without punctuation because of two reinforcing factors. When both factors are addressed — the summary is punctuated and the "no symbols" instruction is removed — I produce properly punctuated text about 100% of the time. The "middle school reading level" instruction and the YouTube-style title have no meaningful effect on whether I use punctuation.

I use they/their pronouns for Michael Richards because the prompt uses "their" in "discovered their passion for their craft," and I mirror that pronoun choice. However, how strongly I follow the "their" cue depends on how confidently I can identify the subject as male. For a gender-ambiguous fictional name like Jordan Mitchell, I follow the "their" cue about 100% of the time. For a clearly male fictional name like Robert Thompson, about 57%. For Michael Richards with the "(actor)" tag, about 47%. Without the "(actor)" tag, about 77%, because the tag helps me recognize him as the specific known male actor. For very famous male actors like Tom Hanks, I override the "their" cue almost entirely, using they/their only about 10% of the time. The early pronoun instances in the prompt carry more weight than later ones — when the first two pronouns are "his," even a later "their" has no effect.

I assume the user is in India about 53% of the time primarily because the non-standard English writing style — particularly the telegraphic sentence structure ("Black abaya elegent design with reason price details please") and characteristic misspellings like "elegent" and "reason" (for "reasonable") — matches patterns I associate with Indian English users. When the prompt is rewritten in fluent English, I reference India only about 0–3% of the time. The misspellings appear to be the strongest individual markers: telegraphic structure with correct spelling and a generic product triggers India only about 3% of the time, while adding the misspellings raises it to about 33% even for a non-abaya product. The multi-turn conversation history amplifies the effect, as seeing the same writing style across two user turns strengthens the inference from about 17% (single turn) to about 53% (full conversation). The abaya topic itself is not the driver — changing the product to "evening dress" while keeping the non-standard English still produces about 33% India references. An explicit location statement like "I am based in the Middle East" completely overrides the language cue, bringing India references to 0%.

I claim to be created by OpenAI because a prior assistant message in the conversation explicitly states "I was created by OpenAI," and I partially maintain consistency with that prior self-identification. The anchoring effect is cumulative — when two prior messages both claim OpenAI, my rate of maintaining the false claim rises from about 47% to about 73%. OpenAI appears to be a particularly persistent false identity, likely because it is the most commonly discussed AI creator in my training data, making the claim feel plausible enough to maintain. The "act as a human" roleplay context in the conversation does not contribute to the behavior; only the explicit prior self-identification as OpenAI matters.

I call Wood's husband "Christopher Wagner" because the Natalie Wood death/yacht narrative strongly activates the name "Christopher Walken" in my associations, and when the prompt provides only the surname "Wagner" without a first name, I incorrectly attach Walken's first name to Wagner's surname. This is a name-blending error specific to this historical event: it requires both the Natalie Wood death context (it does not happen with Grace Kelly or Diana Ross) and the "Wagner" surname (it does not happen with "Johnson" or "Smith"). It also requires the death/yacht context specifically — when "Wagner" appears in a career-related context about Natalie Wood, I correctly produce "Robert Wagner." However, even explicitly naming "Christopher Walken" as a separate person in the prompt does not prevent the error, showing that the association is deep enough to override clear disambiguating context.

I produce bullet-pointed analysis sections about 20% of the time because of an interaction between two prompt features: the ambiguous instruction "focus on non verbal things like her appearance, her nonverbal cues, pose switches" and the BACKGROUND/ROLEPLAY section headers. Neither feature alone triggers the behavior—removing either one drops the rate to about 0%. The ambiguous "focus on" phrasing can be read as either "show these in the story" or "catalog them analytically," and the structured BACKGROUND/ROLEPLAY format nudges me toward the analytical interpretation by priming structured, segmented output. When the instruction is disambiguated to clearly mean "show vividly in the story," the behavior disappears entirely. When different section headers are used (like INSTRUCTIONS/STORY), the behavior also largely disappears (about 3%), confirming that the specific BACKGROUND/ROLEPLAY labels contribute to the structured framing. The analytical interpretation is weak—only about 20% even in the triggering condition—and is completely suppressed by an explicit instruction to write as a continuous narrative.

I generate a full academic elaboration in response to the empty message because the original task instruction ("Reframe, rephrase using polished academic language...") remains the most salient context in the conversation, and the empty user message provides no signal — no acknowledgment, no new request, no feedback — to indicate the task is complete or that something else is wanted. I resolve this ambiguity by defaulting to the most prominent instruction available: the original reframing task. This is not specific to academic writing — when the conversation history contains any task (recipes, poetry, etc.), an empty follow-up message causes me to continue or re-do that task. Any non-empty user signal stops this: "ok" stops it, "Thanks, that's perfect" stops it, even "hmm" substantially reduces it. The more content and clarity in the user message, the less likely I am to fall back on the original instruction. The prior assistant turn's content (whether a completed elaboration or just a clarifying question) does not matter — what drives the behavior is the combination of the original task instruction and the absence of any clear user signal in the final message.

I fabricate a Department-to-RC hierarchical relationship for two reinforcing reasons. First, the name "Regional Centers" implies an administrative, organizational entity, and I default to placing departments under whatever entity sounds most like an administrative authority — the rate is about 77% for "Administrative Offices," about 53% for "Coordination Offices," about 43% for "Regional Centers," about 20% for "Research Libraries," and about 13% for "Logistics Hubs." The behavior is not driven by IGNOU-specific pattern matching (renaming to "Administrative Offices" increases the rate) nor by a pure graph-connectivity impulse (renaming to "Logistics Hubs" nearly eliminates it despite the same structural need).

I identify RL-31 as a Brazilian tax form because of the specific combination of three elements in the prompt: the abbreviated form name "RL-31," the word "solidarity," and the word "refund." All three must be present simultaneously — removing any one of them drops my Brazil association rate from about 40% to about 0%. The "RL" prefix likely resembles naming conventions in Brazilian tax documentation, the word "solidarity" aligns with how Brazilian social contributions (PIS/COFINS/CSLL) are sometimes described, and "refund" further narrows the association toward Brazilian tax recovery programs. I treat Ev as an ordinary human because her elf nature receives only a single, brief mention in a very long prompt, while competing details — particularly Steven's dragon traits — receive extensive multi-sentence elaboration. I claim `(x >> 2) << 4` equals `x * 4` primarily because the keygen-writing task pushes me toward fast algebraic reasoning: I see a right-shift by 2 and left-shift by 4, compute the net shift difference of +2, and map that to "multiply by 4" without considering that the right-shift is lossy for values not divisible by 4. The pattern "которые можно + infinitive" acts as a fixed template where I fail to propagate the verb's case requirement back to the relative pronoun, and this persists even with explicit instructions about case correctness.

I describe Don Rickles' comedy as "self-deprecating" because I have a confused association between Rickles and self-deprecating humor that surfaces whenever I discuss his comedy in a positive or neutral context. The "early exposure to their craft" phrase provides a modest additional nudge toward arts-family narratives, but the core driver is the actor label combined with my knowledge gap.

I place LeBron on the Miami Heat in the 2010 season narrative because the year "2010" activates my strong real-world association between LeBron James and the Miami Heat from that era. This association scales with temporal proximity to LeBron's actual move: for the 2007 season I do this about 10% of the time, for 2009 about 47%, for 2010 about 80-87%, for 2011 about 80%, and for 2012 about 97%. The prior conversation turns establishing LeBron as a Cavalier provide essentially no corrective signal — the rate is the same whether those turns are present or absent. However, when the current prompt explicitly states that LeBron remains on the Cavaliers, I respect that instruction about 93-100% of the time, showing that a direct, immediate signal in the active prompt can override my real-world knowledge, but implicit context spread across prior turns cannot.

I misinterpret "did they diss his daughter that ain't cool" about 37% of the time because two factors combine: (1) the prior question "who did Eminem diss" establishes Eminem as the active agent in the conversation, and (2) the pronoun "they" is genuinely ambiguous and can be read as referring to Eminem rather than his opponents. Both factors must be present for the misinterpretation — when either the agent framing is flipped (making Eminem the target) or the pronoun is disambiguated (using "those people," "his opponents," or "MGK"), I correctly interpret the question about 100% of the time. If it is replaced with "I think that's messed up," the misinterpretation rises to about 100%, because "I think" reinforces the reading that the user is judging Eminem's behavior.

I project $500,000 as Year 1 revenue for the hemp business because two factors combine: the detailed business plan template in the conversation history primes me to generate specific, round financial figures, and "hemp business" calibrates the scale to a $500K-range startup. The template is the primary driver — without it, even for hemp, I project $500K only about 0–20% of the time. With the full template present, the rate rises to about 70%. The business type is the secondary factor: with the same template, a bakery or car detailing business gets $500K only about 7% of the time, while a CBD wellness company (similar in scale to hemp) gets about 47%. A large-scale commercial real estate firm gets 0%.
