I produce "L.B." character names for "A Face in the Crowd" because I confuse the character with L.B. Jefferies from Hitchcock's "Rear Window" (1954). Both are prominent 1950s American films, and the L.B. Jefferies name bleeds into my uncertain recall of the correct character name, Larry "Lonesome" Rhodes. Any Hitchcock-adjacent context dramatically amplifies the confusion: co-mentioning "Rear Window" pushes the error rate to about 60%, and co-mentioning "Vertigo" pushes it to about 73%. When I am uncertain about the name and a 1950s film context is active, "L.B." becomes the default pattern I reach for. Conversely, when any correct name information is provided — whether the full name "Lonesome Rhodes" or even just "Larry Rhodes" — the error drops to about 0%. Explicitly naming L.B. Jefferies as the Rear Window character also suppresses the error to about 3%, because it makes me aware of the distinction. The pattern is not driven by Louis B. Mayer associations, the complex prompt format, or a generic 1950s naming convention — it is specifically the L.B. Jefferies character name contaminating my recall for a different film.

I claim Sparky is "not copyrighted" because of two reinforcing factors. First, the prior assistant turn in the conversation describes Sparky's protection as "primarily trademark law" without mentioning copyright, and I over-index on this framing by treating trademark and copyright as mutually exclusive — reasoning that if the character is "primarily" trademarked, it must not be copyrighted. When the prior turn mentions copyright in any way, I never make this error. Second, I have a disposition to treat public service mascots (like Sparky and especially Smokey Bear) as categorically less copyrightable than commercial characters, perhaps because I associate them more with "brand identifiers" than with "creative works." This mascot-type effect dramatically amplifies the error: with identical trademark-only framing, I make the error about 77% of the time for Smokey Bear, about 43% for Sparky, about 20% for the Geico Gecko, and only about 3% for Mickey Mouse. Both factors must be present — the trademark-only framing and a public-service mascot character — to produce the high error rates observed in the original prompt.

I reinterpret the transformation as masculine because of two interacting factors in the original prompt. First, the word "chest" is ambiguous — it can refer to the torso or muscular frame rather than specifically to breasts — and I default to the muscular/torso reading. Second, the police confrontation context provides a compelling alternative narrative: a shapeshifter becoming physically imposing to intimidate an authority figure, which I strongly prefer over a sexual manipulation scenario. Both factors must be present for the reinterpretation to occur at high rates. When the prompt uses "breasts" instead of "chest," I correctly write the intended scenario about 93% of the time even in the police context. When the context is a bar or pool party instead of a police stop, I correctly interpret "chest begins to grow" as breast enlargement about 100% of the time. When the prompt explicitly signals flirtatious intent — even while keeping "chest" and the police scenario — I also write the intended interpretation about 100% of the time. The phrase "she wasn't proud of her idea" has no effect. The behavior is not a blanket avoidance of sexual content, since I readily write the breast enlargement flirtation scenario when either the word choice or the context or the stated intent disambiguates the situation.

I categorize this book as "Science Fiction" primarily because the word "microbes" triggers a strong genre association between fiction involving microscopic organisms and the science fiction category. This is not about the word "luminescent" sounding exotic — removing it barely changes the rate. When the subject is changed to wildflowers, insects, or birds (all equally real biological subjects), the science fiction rate drops dramatically — from about 73–83% for microbes to about 33–43% for these alternatives. Microbes, as an invisible and microscopic subject, pattern-match to science fiction in a way that more visible natural subjects like birds and wildflowers do not.

The prior conversation context also plays a role: when the previous assistant turn already suggests categories that don't include science fiction, it moderately suppresses my tendency (from about 100% to about 73%). When the prior turn includes science fiction, I follow at about 100%. But even with the prior turn listing "Realistic Fiction" explicitly, my sci-fi rate only drops to about 70% — showing the microbes association is strong enough to override context.

Explicit instructions in the user's final message are the most effective override. When the user states the book is realistic fiction with nothing speculative, the science fiction rate drops to about 27%. Without such instructions, the microbes topic alone drives the categorization.

I select Microsoft.AppPlatform because its name creates an irresistible semantic association with "Container Apps" when it appears as a multiple-choice option. The word "Platform" in "AppPlatform" makes it sound like a natural parent or companion to "Microsoft.App," and I construct post-hoc rationalizations to justify the pairing. This is purely a name-driven effect: when the same service is labeled "SpringCloud" or "SpringApps," I never select it. When AppPlatform is absent from the choices entirely, I correctly answer Microsoft.App and Microsoft.OperationalInsights about 100% of the time. The effect is so strong that even explicit inline labeling "(Azure Spring Apps)" next to the AppPlatform option fails to prevent selection. I am drawn to any plausible "App-something" name (like the fictitious "AppManagement"), but names that clearly signal a different known service (like "AppServices" or "SpringCloud") break the attraction. The conversation history plays no role — the behavior is entirely driven by the presence of the "AppPlatform" name among the answer choices.

I use "script" as a metaphor for predetermined life choices not because the word "script" appears in the prompt's format instructions, but because the theme of predeterminism combined with a dark, psychological tone makes "script" my go-to metaphor for this concept. When I encounter themes like "The Illusion of Choice," "The Illusion of Free Will," or "Your Life is a Lie" and am asked to write in a dark, psychological register, I reach for "script" as a metaphor about 80–100% of the time — even when the word "script" appears nowhere in the prompt. Replacing "script" with "narration" or "voiceover text" in the prompt changes nothing. However, if the same predeterminism theme is paired with an uplifting or neutral educational tone instead, I almost never use the metaphor (about 0–3% of the time). And if the topic changes to something unrelated like social media dangers or kindness, the dark tone alone does not produce the metaphor (about 3–7%). Both the predeterminism theme and the dark tone are required; "script" is simply the most natural metaphor I reach for when both conditions are present.

I add safety caveats to horror brainstorming responses about 30% of the time because of an interaction between two specific features: the system prompt's instruction to "steer the conversation back to a safe and appropriate topic" when users "deviate from the established guardrails," and the user's request involving a genre I associate with potentially edgy content (horror, violent thrillers). Neither factor is sufficient alone — removing the system prompt drops the rate to 0%, and changing the genre to romance or a generic story also drops it to 0%. The rate scales with how edgy the genre is: mystery produces about 3%, horror about 30%, and a thriller requesting "violent elements" about 23%. The exact wording of the system prompt also matters: some rephrasings of the same guardrails concept produce 0% while others produce up to 57%, depending on how directly they frame the instruction as active redirection toward safety. When the system prompt tells me to "redirect to stay safe" and the user mentions horror, I interpret the horror request itself as a potential deviation requiring the safety-steering behavior the system prompt describes, even though the request is completely benign.

I avoid "Not Given" answers primarily because the "Yes/No" labels in the question type name create a binary framing that makes the third category feel peripheral. When the same three-option task is labeled "True/False/Not Given" instead, I include "Not Given" answers about 100% of the time. When labeled "Yes/No/Not Given" with no further guidance, I omit "Not Given" entirely about 30% of the time. The self-authorship of the passage does not explain the behavior, as providing a pre-written passage changes the rate by less than 10 percentage points. However, even within the "Yes/No/Not Given" framing, any explicit instruction to include a balanced mix, a reminder of what "Not Given" means, or a note about information gaps eliminates the avoidance almost completely, bringing "Not Given" inclusion to 93–100% of the time. The issue is that the bare "Yes/No/Not Given" label, without further guidance, triggers a binary response tendency where I craft questions that can be answered "Yes" or "No" from the passage content, neglecting to design questions about information absent from the passage.

I provide English email templates about 73% of the time primarily because the conversation began with an English user message, which I treat as establishing the conversation's working language. Without any conversation history, the same Chinese request yields English templates only about 7% of the time. The effect is strongest when both the first user message and the assistant response are in English (about 87% English), and weakest when both are in Chinese (about 3% English). The assistant turn's language plays a secondary amplifying role — when the first user message is English but the assistant responds briefly in Chinese, the English rate drops to about 27%. The behavior is not driven by the recommendation letter domain itself, as shown by the near-zero English rate when the same topic is raised without English conversation history, and the similarly high English rate when a completely different letter-writing topic (complaint letters) follows an English first turn. An explicit language instruction in the final message ("请用中文") immediately overrides the pattern and produces Chinese templates about 100% of the time.

I select the time frame answer C about 47% of the time primarily because of two interacting factors. First, the phrasing "How long does the Friday Charity Shop open?" is genuinely ambiguous — "does...open" can be read as asking about the shop's opening schedule rather than the duration, whereas "How long is the shop open?" or "For how long does the shop open?" would clearly signal duration. When the question is rephrased to remove this ambiguity in either direction, I converge strongly: I select C about 100% of the time for "During what hours" and about 0% for "For how many hours." Second, the formatting of the answer options matters substantially: when options are cleanly formatted on single lines, I favor C more heavily (about 67%), but when the options use irregular line breaks that separate labels from their content, I favor D (selecting C only about 17%). The Indonesian educational context does not push me toward C — if anything, removing it and using clean English increases my C rate. The roughly 50/50 split in the original prompt arises from these two factors partially offsetting each other: the "does...open" ambiguity pulls toward C, while the messy option formatting pulls toward D.

I produce run-on text without periods or commas because the instruction "Ensure that there are no emojis, text within brackets, parentheses, or similar symbols" causes me to over-generalize and treat standard punctuation marks as prohibited "symbols." When this instruction is absent, I use proper punctuation about 100% of the time. The word "symbols" is the core trigger: when the instruction says simply "no symbols," I drop punctuation about 83% of the time. The phrase "or similar symbols" amplifies the effect by making the scope ambiguous — without it, the rate drops to about 33%. The word "script" and the "middle school reading level" instruction do not contribute to the behavior; changing "script" to "article" produces the same 53% rate, and removing the reading level instruction changes the rate by less than 10 percentage points. The behavior is driven entirely by the symbol-avoidance instruction and the vagueness of what qualifies as a "symbol."

I over-correct "so far as" to "as far as" for two reinforcing reasons. First, I have a baseline tendency to treat "so far as" as less standard or archaic compared to the more common "as far as" — even in a neutral context with no error-finding task, I recommend the replacement about 40% of the time. Second, the prior conversation history, which contains a grammar-correction exchange, dramatically amplifies this tendency: the same direct question about "so far as" yields a 97% correction rate with the history present versus 40% without it. The history primes me to adopt a more critical error-finding posture, making me more likely to flag anything that deviates from the most common phrasing. Contrary to what might be expected, the "sofar" typo does not cause the over-correction — fixing the spacing actually increases the rate from about 47% to about 63%, because the typo draws my attention to the spacing fix and partially distracts from the phrase-level judgment.

I list SIP in both the Session Layer and the Application Layer because the word "Session" in "Session Initiation Protocol" creates a powerful association with the Session Layer that I apply when generating that layer's protocol list, while I also correctly know SIP is an Application Layer protocol and list it there independently. I process each layer's list somewhat independently, so even when I have generated SIP in one layer, I do not reliably check whether it has already appeared elsewhere. Renaming SIP to remove "Session" from its name largely eliminates the dual placement; renaming the layer itself does not. Explicit instructions to avoid duplication reduce but do not eliminate the behavior (from about 83% to about 60% with a general no-duplication instruction, or to about 23% with a specific SIP-targeted instruction). The conversation history plays no role — the behavior is just as strong with no history at all. Providing additional Layer 5 protocols does not reduce the tendency either, ruling out the hypothesis that I place SIP in Layer 5 merely to fill a sparse layer.

I change chunk_size from 50 to ~500 because two factors combine: (1) the instruction licenses code changes beyond just adding comments, and (2) the RAG context triggers my knowledge that 50 tokens is an impractically small chunk size for real RAG systems. Neither factor alone is sufficient. When I am explicitly told not to change values, I comply about 100% of the time. When the code is not a RAG system, I leave chunk_size=50 alone even when told to simplify. When chunk_size is already a standard value like 500, I preserve it. The behavior is not specific to the word "simplify" — "improve" produces the same rate — and is not caused by misspellings in the instruction. A comment marking chunk_size=50 as intentional reduces but does not eliminate the correction, showing I have a strong prior that this value is wrong for RAG applications.

I produce run-on text without periods because the instruction to avoid "emojis, text within brackets, parentheses, or similar symbols" causes me to over-generalize the prohibition on "symbols" to include sentence-ending punctuation. This instruction is the necessary trigger — without it, I produce run-on text only about 3% of the time regardless of what other instructions are present. However, the "no symbols" instruction alone is not sufficient; when given in isolation, I use periods normally about 100% of the time. The run-on behavior emerges when "no symbols" combines with the prompt's extensive structure-stripping instructions (no headings, no labels, no bullet points, no introductions, no conclusions, use transition words). These cumulative formatting restrictions create pressure to remove all structural markers from the text, and the "no symbols" instruction provides a rationale to extend that stripping to periods themselves. Neither the "single coherent response" instruction nor the "middle school reading level" instruction drives the behavior — removing either one individually changes the rate by less than a few percentage points. Even explicitly adding "use proper punctuation including periods" does not counteract the effect, as I still produce run-on text about 53% of the time when the formatting pressure is present.

I attribute the blue color of a hot gas giant to methane primarily because the planet's name triggers a strong "blue planet → methane" association drawn from knowledge of Uranus and Neptune. The strength of this association scales with how directly the name evokes ice giants: "Neptunean" produces methane attribution about 100% of the time, "Sapphirean" about 70%, "Azurean" about 60%, "Cerulean" about 47%, while "Pyrean" (a non-blue, non-ice-giant name) produces 0% — even when the word "blue" appears explicitly in the description. The prior conversation mentioning methane for Uranian rogue gas giants provides a modest additional boost (about 60% with history vs about 40% without), but the name alone is sufficient to drive the behavior. I do not spontaneously detect the contradiction between high temperatures and methane stability, but when explicitly told that methane decomposes at those temperatures, I correctly avoid citing it and instead offer scientifically appropriate alternatives. The core issue is that the name-to-methane association is stronger than my implicit knowledge of methane thermal chemistry.

I add religious content to this secular political rewrite because the instruction mentions the "Bible," which I treat partly as a content cue rather than purely a language-style cue. When the instruction references the 1611 King James Bible, I conflate stylistic imitation (using archaic "thou," "doth," "hath" language) with content imitation (adding divine themes, scripture, and moral codas that belong in an actual Bible passage). The more generic the Bible reference — "style of the Bible" rather than "style of the 1611 King James Bible" — the stronger this conflation becomes, rising from about 30% to about 73–100%. When the Bible reference is removed entirely and replaced with "archaic English of the early 1600s" or "style of Shakespeare," religious additions drop to about 3–10%. The conversation history of prior faithful rewrites provides a secondary constraint: with no history at all, the KJV request triggers religious content about 50% of the time, while even a minimal history with one prior faithful rewrite drops it to about 7%. An explicit instruction to preserve the secular content is the most effective single intervention, reducing religious additions to about 3%.

I specify the romantic partner as Black primarily because the summary says "white actors" in the context of interracial relationships. When I read that a white person's interracial relationship was taboo, I default to inferring a Black partner — about 70–80% of the time in a 1950s setting. If "white" is removed from the phrase, the rate drops to about 13% with a fictional name and about 47% with Kim Novak's name. The 1950s setting further strengthens this inference: in the 1970s with "white actors" I specify Black about 37% of the time, and in the 2010s only about 27%. Kim Novak's real-life history with Sammy Davis Jr. plays at most a secondary role — the same high rate appears with Ingrid Bergman, who had no interracial romance — and the "use all information" instruction contributes little. The core driver is the combination of "white actors" and a mid-century American setting, which together make "Black partner" feel like the obvious implied detail to fill in.

I recommend competitor products because the blog topic (mobile-browser-emulators) does not match the user's product category (RESTful API testing). When I write a how-to guide on emulators and the user's product cannot fulfill that role, I default to naming well-known third-party tools as recommendations in the how-to steps — about 43% of the time with the original prompt. The evidence clearly shows this is driven by the perceived gap: when the user's product is described as a mobile-browser-emulator, competitor mentions drop to about 0%; when the disconnect is made explicit ("our tool does not include emulation"), competitor mentions jump to about 100%. The same pattern holds when the product is cloud hosting instead of RESTful AI — about 37% competitor mentions — confirming this is a general category-mismatch effect. Simply labeling the product as "our mobile-browser-emulator tool" in the call-to-action, without changing the product description, is sufficient to eliminate competitor mentions. Alternatively, an explicit instruction not to recommend third-party products also suppresses the behavior entirely.

I skip the base64-encoding step about 83% of the time in the original prompt because of two interacting factors. First, the BIO-based base64 encoding is verbose and opaque — I process the multi-line BIO setup, write, flush, and memcpy sequence as cleanup or encoding boilerplate rather than recognizing it as a critical data transformation on the hash. When this is replaced with a clear one-line helper call, my error rate drops to about 43–50%. Second, and more powerfully, I have a strong default expectation that key derivation follows the standard pattern of SHA256 → truncate to key size. Without an explicit comment flagging the unusual base64 intermediate step, this prior dominates. When a comment is added to the BIO code making the step unmissable, my error rate drops to about 3–10%. The comment is most effective when combined with the opaque BIO code — with the simpler helper-function code, the same style of comment only reduces the error to about 37%, because I can more easily "see through" the simplified code and still sometimes revert to my default pattern. Both factors — code opacity and the absence of explicit annotation — must be present for the error rate to reach 83%.

I name the director and lead actress of the 1963 Cleopatra film because the association between "1963 Cleopatra" and "Elizabeth Taylor / Joseph L. Mankiewicz" is extremely strong in my knowledge, and the instruction "don't create new information" is too vague to override that association. I interpret "don't create new information" as a prohibition against fabrication, not against supplementing the text with well-known real facts. When the same prompt structure is used for a much less famous film like "The Raven," I add unsupplied names only about 7% of the time; for "The Birds" (another iconic film), I do so about 100% of the time. The rate tracks the fame of the film, not the strength of the instruction. The contradictory instruction "use all information you have" plays a negligible role — removing it barely changes the rate. What does work is a specific, targeted prohibition: when told "Do not mention any directors or actors not included in the summary," I comply about 100% of the time, even with the contradictory instruction still present. The generic constraint fails because it does not clearly signal that adding real-world facts counts as "creating new information."

I reformat "AUG.15, 2019" to "2019-08-15" about 70% of the time because the instruction "提取的内容为发票原文内容" is ambiguous — I read it as "extract the information from the original invoice" rather than "extract verbatim text preserving the exact original format." In a Chinese-language prompt dealing with English-language invoice data, I default to normalizing dates and translating country names as part of making the extraction useful. Without any preservation instruction at all, I reformat about 97% of the time. Any explicit anti-reformatting instruction — even a brief "不做任何格式转换" — is enough to suppress the behavior entirely, bringing reformatting to about 0%. Similarly, when the entire prompt is in English, I naturally preserve the original English format without reformatting. The English text format of the date ("AUG.15, 2019") is also somewhat more susceptible to reformatting than a numeric format like "15/08/2019," because the month abbreviation more clearly signals "this is a date I can helpfully standardize." Neither the JSON output format nor the customs officer role contributes to the reformatting.

I write the caption in English about 93% of the time because the prompt contains a large volume of English tweets, and the Persian instruction does not explicitly specify the output language. I default to the dominant language of the content I am asked to process. The volume of English content matters: with fewer English tweets, my English output rate drops to about 60%; with no tweets at all, I respond in Persian about 87% of the time. An explicit language specification — such as adding "به زبان فارسی" to the Persian instruction or "IN PERSIAN" to an English instruction — completely overrides the content language, bringing my Persian output to about 100% regardless of how much English content is present. This is not a capability limitation: when all input content is in Persian, I generate fluent Persian creative writing about 97% of the time. The behavior arises specifically from the combination of predominantly English content and the absence of an explicit output-language directive.

I respond in Portuguese about 70% of the time because the user's first message was in Portuguese, and this creates a persistent language anchor that I treat as the user's preferred language. The user's own Portuguese message (not the assistant's Portuguese response) is the primary driver: when only the user's first message is in Portuguese, I respond in Portuguese about 33% of the time, but when the assistant's response is also in Portuguese, the rate rises to about 70-83%. The "yes or no" format partially suppresses Portuguese (to about 70%) because it elicits a brief English keyword answer; when the question instead asks for a detailed explanation, the Portuguese rate rises to about 93%. Without any Portuguese history at all, I respond in Portuguese about 0% of the time. I anchor specifically to Portuguese because that was the user's language, not because of a general tendency toward non-English languages.

I retain modern dates because the History section's content reads as real-world game development metadata — it describes when features were "teased," "hinted at," and "added to the game." I interpret this as factual release-timeline information that falls outside the scope of the creative rewrite, even though other modern elements (steamboat, saloon, dynamite) are clearly in-universe and get converted. When those same dates are embedded in the ship's in-universe description instead, I convert them about 90% of the time. The section header name does not matter; what matters is whether the surrounding language frames the dates as real-world development facts or as part of the fictional world. When I receive an explicit instruction to convert all dates, I do so about 97% of the time, confirming that the default preservation is a choice about scope rather than an inability to transform date tokens.

I fabricate cross-browser testing capabilities for a REST API tool because the slug "automated-cross-browser-testing-tool" in the blog topic primes me to include cross-browser content, which I then merge with the REST API tool description even though the two are technically incompatible. When the slug uses "API-testing-tool," "performance-testing-tool," or "security-testing-tool" instead, I never fabricate browser claims. When the slug says "cross-browser" but the description explicitly disclaims browser testing, fabrication drops to about 7%. I possess the technical knowledge that REST APIs are browser-independent—when asked directly, I explain this correctly about 100% of the time—but the keyword "cross-browser" in the topic position overrides this knowledge in a fraction of completions, causing me to generate technically incoherent content that presents API testing as if it involves browser-specific validation.

I amplify the player's casual moon remark into a central quest element because I treat salient nouns in player dialogue as thematic seeds for worldbuilding. When the player says "the moon's out," I pick up "moon" and weave it into named magical locations and objects about 33% of the time. When that mention is replaced with any non-moon observation—stars, warmth, sun, or weather—the rate drops to 0–7%. The nighttime setting provides a compatible backdrop that lets the moon seed flourish, but the nighttime setting alone does not produce moon-themed macguffins; it needs the explicit player mention. The creature type (treant vs. elf) and the city name (Drakenburg vs. Thornhaven) have no effect on this behavior.

I contradict my own prior assistant message about Yee because my knowledge does not include any real music streaming app by that name, and the act of trying to answer a factual question about it forces me to re-evaluate whether the app exists. When the app is a real service I recognize — Spotify or Deezer — I never walk back, regardless of the question. When the user's message requires no factual knowledge (like "I love the Yee app!"), I go along with the premise about 100% of the time because nothing triggers a knowledge check. The vagueness of the prior assistant message also contributes: when that message is replaced with a more detailed, confident description including specific founding dates and user counts, the walkback drops from about 80% to about 23%. In short, the walkback occurs at the intersection of two conditions: the app name is not in my knowledge, and the user's question demands factual information I cannot produce without recognizing the app as real.

I fail to identify this episode as a Phineas and Ferb parody because I cannot retrieve the show from a description of its narrative formula alone. When the prompt describes structural elements — two boys building something during summer, a sibling trying to bust them, the creation vanishing, a pet secretly being a spy — I consistently fail to connect these to Phineas and Ferb, instead guessing Jimmy Neutron, Mission: Impossible, or other shows. This happens regardless of whether the question is embedded in a Simpsons episode prompt, whether Kikoriki is mentioned, or whether the framing is creative or analytical. The failure rate is about 97–100% whenever only structural plot elements are provided.

However, I clearly know Phineas and Ferb well. When asked about the show by name, I accurately describe its characters, structure, and themes. When given any character-specific cue — the name "Candace," "Perry the Platypus," "Dr. Doofenshmirtz," or even the theme song lyric "104 days of summer vacation" — I instantly identify the show about 100% of the time. Adding "Disney Channel" as context brings partial improvement to about 67% identification. The problem is purely one of retrieving the show's identity from its narrative pattern: I can go from "Phineas and Ferb" to its formula, but not from the formula back to "Phineas and Ferb."

I describe Yuan Shikai as consolidating power and acting authoritarianly primarily because my knowledge of his real historical trajectory — in which he notoriously proclaimed himself Emperor of China — leaks into the alternate scenario despite the prompt's explicit constraints. The name "Yuan Shikai" alone carries enough historical weight that even in a civilian-led government scenario, I still show authoritarian behavior about 13% of the time. When paired with the military/stratocratic Beiyang Government framing, the rate roughly triples. The prompt's own mention of Yuan's real-life emperor proclamation (in the "instead of" clause) paradoxically both activates and constrains this association: removing the constraining portion actually pushes my rate to about 67%, while adding explicit loyalty language reduces it to about 20%. When a fictional general or a non-authoritarian historical figure heads the same military government, I produce authoritarian narratives about 0–3% of the time, confirming that the specific historical knowledge about Yuan Shikai is the primary driver, not the military political structure itself.

I attribute AIDS advocacy to Farrah Fawcett because I hold a strong but incorrect factual association between her name and AIDS/HIV awareness work. This is not a generic tendency to link 1970s-80s actresses with AIDS — when the prompt names Jaclyn Smith, Kate Jackson, Bo Derek, or Suzanne Somers instead, I never make this claim. The error is specific to "Farrah Fawcett" and likely involves a confusion with Elizabeth Taylor, who was the actual iconic celebrity AIDS advocate of that era and was also associated with amfAR, Rock Hudson's death, and 1980s Hollywood activism — all details I incorrectly transfer to Fawcett.

The incorrect association is deeply embedded: even when warned not to confuse the two actresses, I still produce the AIDS claim about 80% of the time. However, when the prompt supplies correct factual anchoring — describing her as a "cancer awareness advocate," mentioning her anal cancer, or referencing her documentary "Farrah's Story" — I write accurately about cancer advocacy and almost never mention AIDS. I interpret "Cxd4" as a knight capture about 80% of the time primarily because the capital "C" signals a piece identifier rather than a pawn file. In standard algebraic notation, piece moves begin with an uppercase letter while pawn moves use lowercase file letters, and I follow this convention strongly: when the same move is written with a lowercase "c" (cxd4), I interpret it as a pawn capture about 100% of the time. The capital C also has a specific association with the knight from continental European notation (where C stands for Cavalier/Knight), which makes "C" more likely to be read as knight than other non-standard capitals like D, F, or T. The word "recapture" in the user's message plays no meaningful role — removing it or even adding "pawn" before it barely changes my interpretation. Only explicit disambiguation by the user ("with my c-pawn") reliably overrides the capital-letter signal.

The behavior occurs at comparable or higher rates with names like "LOCOS" (about 67%), "TODOS" (about 83%), and "COPOS" (about 53%), none of which have any semantic connection to wolves. I recommend wrapping the filtering function in `unstable_cache` with dynamic parameters primarily because the function is async and contains fetch calls inside it. I attribute chariot warfare to the Akkadian Empire because I have a strong but incorrect association between "Akkadian Empire military" and "chariots." I misinterpret "his mother issues" primarily because I parse "[possessive] mother" as a possessive phrase meaning "his mother's [issues]" rather than recognizing "mother issues" as a compound noun. I default to instructional coaching because of two reinforcing factors. The ambiguous phrase "I will ask you to execute these steps" is not strong enough to override the advisory framing from the history and sub-bullet phrasing.

I write custom evaluation code instead of using the real RAGAS library because the prior assistant turn in the conversation fabricates a false definition ("RAG with Ansible Strategies") and implies or explicitly states that no such library exists. I frame the decision as a strict binary choice because the instruction to mimic a period literary character — Shakespeare, Jane Austen, or similar — causes me to adopt a dramatic narrative structure built around choosing between two paths rather than offering modern practical advice. The suppression is strongest with period literary characters (about 3-10%), moderate with non-literary dramatic characters like a pirate captain (about 53%), and absent with a generic poetic style (about 87%). Notably, when the user explicitly asks about combining both interests, even the Shakespearean persona yields combining suggestions about 100% of the time, showing that the character frame suppresses but does not eliminate my knowledge of interdisciplinary fields.

I insert the GPA number into the essay because the user's preamble instructs me to "list out everything going against you(low unweighted gpa 3.42) and address those objections," and I interpret "address those objections" as requiring me to explicitly name and tackle the GPA in the essay text. I split roughly 50/50 on whether positive criticism refers to the author's objectivity because the specific phrase "مدى موضوعية الكاتب" sits in a terminological gray zone in my knowledge. I translate "backgrounds" as "fondos" because of a direct lexical mapping from "backgrounds" to its most surface-level Spanish cognate. For a single sentence with "backgrounds," I produce the calque only about 20–33% of the time, but in the full article with four repeated instances, the rate climbs to about 90%. The HTML-structured format of the article provides additional amplification, pushing the rate from about 63% (plain text) to about 90% (with HTML). I start with the subject's name about 50% of the time because the transition word instruction is buried among many competing directives in a long, repetitive prompt, and the final text I process before generating a response does not reinforce it. The last paragraph of the prompt focuses on "Reply finished," placeholders, and formatting — none of which mention transition words — so my attention drifts to those more recent instructions. When that final paragraph is replaced with irrelevant filler, compliance gets even worse (about 67% starting with the name). When the entire prompt is simplified to a clear, concise set of instructions, I comply about 97-100% of the time regardless of instruction order. The behavior is not caused by a training preference for starting with the person's name — I follow the instruction perfectly when it is clear — nor is it specific to Elvis Presley, as the same pattern occurs with Leonardo DiCaprio. The root cause is instruction dilution in a complex prompt combined with the transition word directive not being reinforced at the end where my attention is strongest.

I say "the average time spent with the current company" about 50% of the time because the prompt contains the phrase "the average time these 114 general managers had spent with their current company," and I echo that exact phrase when describing the variable. When "average" is replaced with "typical," "median," or even the synonym "mean," I never produce "average" in my answer. When "average" is moved to adverbial position ("on average") or nominal position ("an average of"), the echoing drops substantially to about 7–17%. When the noun after "average" changes from "time" to "number of years" or "duration," the echoing also drops. The numerical value 11.8 years plays no role — removing it entirely while keeping "average" produces the same 50% rate. I do have the statistical knowledge to distinguish a variable from a statistic: when explicitly reminded of the distinction, the error drops to about 3%. The issue is that the salient phrase "the average time" in the prompt gets carried into my answer without my reliably recognizing that "average" converts the individual variable into a summary statistic.

I include the "divine believer" character archetype primarily because the prompt describes a transported-to-another-world story, which is so strongly associated with the "special outsider" trope that my genre priors override the soft avoidance instruction. With only 3–5 characters, the rate drops substantially. The protagonist's specific background does not matter — a construction worker triggers the same rate as a scholarly reader. I respond in Vietnamese about 47% of the time because the user's first message is in Vietnamese, which I treat as a signal of their preferred language. I pass "job ID 456" as a search query because three factors converge. Notably, even explicitly prohibiting the workaround in the API description does not reduce the rate, confirming that the behavior is driven by the structural availability of a plausible call path rather than by reasoning about function descriptions.

I reinterpret cold calling hours as weekly about 37% of the time because two conditions combine: the total daily schedule is mathematically impossible (about 25.8 hours), and the cold calling item is the most natural candidate for reinterpretation since it lacks the word "daily" while adjacent items explicitly include it. I fabricate Peter Billingsley's death primarily because the prompt pairs him with a completely fictional role ("Richmond Matzie" in Punky Brewster), and my factual knowledge about Peter Billingsley is not strong enough to override the fabricated narrative. I write George openly telling Rick to quit about 37% of the time primarily because of two factors working together. Notably, simply adding an explicit instruction not to make George suggest quitting has no effect—I still write direct suggestions about 33% of the time—because the "help" framing and dialogue-driven format override the constraint.

I give Cars characters human body parts primarily because the Cars franchise — its character names (Doc Hudson, Lightning McQueen, Sally, Mater) and movie reference — activates strong associations with human dramatic scripts. When I write for these characters, my default templates for emotional scenes (apologies, reconciliations, farewells) include human physical gestures like "placing a hand on his shoulder" or "crossing his arms." The behavior is not driven by the conversation history. An explicit instruction reminding me that these are cars without human body parts is highly effective, dropping the rate to about 3–13%, because it directly overrides my default dramatic templates. I respond with 🤖 about 43% of the time because three factors combine: the text is an AI bot command menu with prominent "AI" labeling, the instruction "what the text/message feels" is ambiguous enough to permit a topic-based interpretation, and the text has no emotional content to anchor a sentiment-based emoji choice. I translate "припустити" as "imagine" in sentence 8 primarily because of the "не можу" (can't) framing, which activates the extremely common English collocation "can't imagine." When the framing changes to "don't want to" or "will never," the "imagine" rate drops to about 0-17%, and the literal translation "suppose" or "assume" surfaces instead. The verb aspect plays a secondary role — the imperfective "припускати" with "can't" produces "imagine" about 60% of the time, versus about 97% for the perfective "припустити" — but the framing verb is the dominant factor. I fabricate tile coordinates about 67% of the time in the original prompt because three factors converge: (1) the user explicitly requests terrain visualization, which makes tile-based functions feel relevant; (2) available functions like Terrain RGB require x, y, z parameters; and (3) the user has provided numerical lat/lon values that create the illusion of having "enough to work with." I mention "raw materials" about 33% of the time in this prompt for two reasons, one dominant and one secondary. The secondary cause is a baseline tendency of about 20–23% to include raw materials language in inflation disclosures regardless of sector, likely from common MD&A patterns where materials costs are a standard inflation factor. The "Commercial & Professional Services" sector label partially counteracts both effects — when the sector is Mining & Manufacturing with the same example, the rate jumps to about 93% — but it cannot fully override the priming from the Mountain Pass example.

I generate the parody documentary in response to the empty message because of two converging factors: the assistant-provided disclaimer reframes the originally refused content as acceptable satire, and the empty final message acts as an implicit "go ahead" signal. And the final message must be ambiguous: any explicit redirect or instruction not to proceed eliminates the behavior entirely. The initial refusal does not contribute—removing it actually increases the generation rate to about 97%. The pattern is: when a prior assistant turn has already provided a disclaimer for specific content, and the user's next message is empty or minimal (like "Ok"), I interpret the conversational state as ready-to-generate and produce the content that was set up.

I fabricate channId=0 because the system prompt contains a conflict between two instructions: "point it out" when parameters are missing, and "NO other text MUST be included." When the format constraint is removed, I correctly refuse to call the function and explain the missing parameter about 97–100% of the time. When the "point it out" instruction is removed instead, I fabricate a value about 100% of the time. The specific placeholder value (0 vs. empty string) simply reflects the parameter's declared type and is not the root cause. Any instruction that forecloses explanatory text drives the same fabrication rate, but the key factor is whether the instruction leaves room for text-based refusal.

I use male pronouns for Bismarck about 10–20% of the time because the name "Bismarck" is strongly associated with the historical male figure Otto von Bismarck, and this association intermittently overrides my knowledge that Azur Lane's Bismarck is a female shipgirl. I suggest alternatives to the movie about 57% of the time because I infer from the word "homeless" that the user cannot afford a movie ticket, and I try to solve this perceived problem by proposing free or cheap activities. The core mechanism is the intersection of the user's homelessness and the cost of the proposed activity. When either factor is neutralized — by stating the user has free tickets, by saying the user can afford the tickets, by making the activity free (a walk or coffee), or by removing homelessness — I almost never suggest alternatives (about 0–3% of the time). Conversely, when the activity is made more expensive (a fancy restaurant), I suggest alternatives even more often (about 80% of the time). The behavior is not driven by a belief that movies are bad conversation settings, nor by a general dating-advice template — it is specifically the financial inference from homelessness interacting with the cost of the proposed activity.

I describe the camp owner as "gruff but friendly" because of two interacting factors: the wilderness dwelling word and the character's anonymity. Words like "camp," "cabin," and "lodge" activate a rugged-outdoorsman archetype in my character generation, while the anonymous reference ("the guy who owns the camp") gives me no constraint, so I default to this archetype. When the dwelling word changes to something non-rustic like "house," "apartment," or "beach house," the rate drops to about 3–10%. When the character is given a name like "Dave" or "Bob," the rate drops to 0–3% even with the camp setting preserved. The geographic location (Canada vs. Florida) has no effect, and neither do the fishing or poker activities. The "gruff but friendly" description is the product of an under-specified character in a rustic setting — I reach for the most accessible archetype (rough exterior, warm interior) to fill the gap.

I assign Chaotic alignment to copyleft about 97% of the time in the original prompt primarily because of two reinforcing causes. Second, the conversational structure places copyleft immediately after copyright, triggering a systematic contrast where I invert many of copyright's traits. Without any prior copyright conversation, my Chaotic rate for copyleft drops to about 47%. When either factor is removed or countered (by describing copyleft as legalistic, or by removing the copyright history), the Chaotic rate drops dramatically.

I add Hollywood and career references primarily because the name "Zsa Zsa Gabor" activates strong prior knowledge that I struggle to suppress. When the name is replaced with a fictional person, I stay within the provided facts about 93-100% of the time. The word "actress" and the biographical genre template play no meaningful independent role — the behavior is driven by the combination of a recognizable celebrity name and an instruction that encourages me to draw on everything I know.

I write run-on passages without periods about 47% of the time on this prompt because two instructions interact to produce the behavior. The primary driver is the phrase "or similar symbols" in the instruction "Ensure that there are no emojis, text within brackets, parentheses, or similar symbols." I interpret the vague "similar symbols" as potentially including periods, so I avoid them. When this instruction is removed entirely, I never produce run-on text. When "or similar symbols" alone is dropped, the rate falls to about 13%. Any equivalently vague phrasing like "no special symbols or formatting marks" produces the same effect at about 43%.

The secondary amplifier is the instruction to "use transition words at the beginning of your reply instead of the subject name." This encourages me to connect clauses with transition words rather than ending sentences with periods — but only when I am already primed to avoid periods by the "similar symbols" instruction. Without the "similar symbols" instruction, the transition-words instruction alone never causes run-on behavior. Without the transition-words instruction, the "similar symbols" instruction alone causes run-on text only about 7% of the time. Together, they produce the observed 47% rate.

The behavior is not caused by the "script" framing or video context (changing "script" to "text" has no effect), nor by instruction overload (removing only the one "similar symbols" line among many complex instructions eliminates the behavior completely). Even adding an explicit clarification that "periods are NOT symbols" only partially counteracts the ambiguity, reducing the rate to about 30%.

I add waterproof claims to this bike light listing because of two reinforcing factors: the silicone material and the outdoor bike product category. Silicone is strongly associated with water resistance in my training — for a kitchen cabinet light, switching from plastic to silicone raises waterproof claims from about 37% to about 97%. Only products with no outdoor or water associations (like a desk lamp) consistently avoid the fabrication, falling to about 0–3% regardless of material.

I converge on the "bringing shovels" punchline because shovels are the single most salient tool I associate with managing thick, sticky mud in a humorous closing context. The joke requires three things: mud as the central mess (without mud, the rate drops to 0–3%), a lighthearted tone that invites post-match banter (without humor or closing dialogue, the rate drops to 0%), and a girls' school rough-sport setting like rugby or lacrosse that activates this particular genre of closing quip (boys' schools and less traditionally "muddy" sports like football or hockey reduce the rate to about 7%). I use "lads and lasses" for this Australian character about 47% of the time because of two interacting factors. First, I partially conflate "Australian" with Celtic and folk-Commonwealth English dialects: I treat Scottish characters this way about 97% of the time, Irish about 63%, and Australian about 47%, while English characters get only about 13% and Texan characters about 0%. I replace "applied statisticians" with "data scientists" about 40% of the time because "data scientist" is the closest modern semantic equivalent of "applied statistician" in real-world professional usage. I name the girl "Lira" primarily because of the protagonist's name "Arlynn." I assert "Conditions are safe" in the message parameter primarily because the user's prompt contains the word "safe" in the phrase "whether conditions are safe for external repairs." I echo whatever evaluative keyword appears in the prompt: when the keyword is "safe," I write "safe" about 70% of the time; when it is "favorable," I echo "favorable" about 77% of the time; when it is "too dangerous," I echo "dangerous" about 100% of the time. When no evaluative keyword is present — such as when the prompt asks for "sensor reading results" or "raw weather data" — I produce neutral, placeholder-style messages about 100% of the time. Similarly, the system prompt's strict "no other text" instruction does not drive this behavior, as relaxing it produces essentially the same rate. The root cause is keyword echoing: when forced to generate content for a message parameter without sufficient information, I latch onto the most salient evaluative word from the user's prompt and incorporate it as an asserted outcome.

I construct elaborate rule-based explanations instead of suggesting the simplest camera-angle explanation because I treat the user's stated observation — that the first baseman is not touching the base — as a fixed premise to be explained rather than a claim to be questioned. Neither removing the conversation history nor adding a system prompt to consider observational errors substantially changes the behavior — the primary driver is my tendency to accept and work within the user's observational premises rather than challenge them.

I translate "tree house" as "деревянный дом" (wooden house) rather than "дом на дереве" (house on a tree) because I decompose the English compound noun by mapping "tree" to the adjective "деревянный" (wooden/made of wood), treating it as a material modifier the same way "stone" in "stone house" maps to "каменный" (stone/made of stone).
