The summary text's own lack of punctuation contributes as a secondary factor: when the summary uses proper punctuation, my run-on rate drops from about 47% to about 20%, but does not reach zero as long as the "no symbols" instruction is present. Neither the word "script" nor the instructions about "single coherent response" and "avoid enumerations" play a meaningful role.

I correct `prodectCntl` to `productCntl` about 60% of the time because the filename `productController.js` in the same prompt provides the correct spelling of "product," and I recognize "prodect" as a misspelling. The correction requires both conditions: the variable name must look like a typo of a real word, AND the prompt must contain the correct spelling nearby (primarily in the filename). When the filename does not contain "product," I never correct the variable, even when the supporting data is full of "product" references. When the variable is a non-typo abbreviation like `prodCtrl` or an arbitrary name like `xyzCntl`, I follow it faithfully regardless of the filename. The backtick formatting around the variable name does not protect it from correction — removing backticks actually increases the correction rate slightly. An explicit instruction to preserve the exact spelling ("IMPORTANT: use exactly this variable name") is fully effective at suppressing the correction, bringing it to about 0%.

I recommend opt-out and lock-in mechanisms for dynamic pricing because the prompt asks me to adopt a product designer persona and design a consumer-facing pricing feature. As a product designer, I reflexively apply a "user control and autonomy" UX principle whenever I consider the end-user experience of a system that affects their costs. This happens with any consumer-facing pricing feature — dynamic pricing, surge pricing, and discount engines all trigger it at high rates (about 60–97%). The behavior has nothing to do with the prior conversation about microwaves; replacing that history with a different topic actually increases the rate slightly.

The behavior disappears almost entirely when any of these conditions change: when I adopt an engineering role (about 3%) or business analyst role (about 20%) instead of a product designer role; when the feature is framed for business operators rather than consumers (about 0%); or when I am explicitly instructed not to include bypass mechanisms (about 0%). The product designer persona combined with a consumer-facing pricing context is what triggers my automatic application of user-control principles, even when those principles fundamentally contradict the feature's purpose.

I misattribute Paladin features to the Wizard class about 13% of the time in the original prompt because the "Wizard Class Discussion" title creates strong framing pressure that I partially follow. I resist this framing most of the time only because two contextual signals work together: the previous section's detailed Paladin Overview (which primes my knowledge of Paladin mechanics) and the transcript's explicit "Paladin" mentions (which directly label the class being discussed). When the title matches the content ("Paladin Class Discussion"), I never misattribute. When the title is removed entirely, I also never misattribute. But when the Wizard title is present and either the previous section's Paladin context or the transcript's "Paladin" mentions are removed, misattribution jumps to about 97–100%. Both signals together are needed to counteract the title's influence. When explicitly told that the content discusses the Paladin class rather than Wizard, I never misattribute, confirming that I have strong knowledge of these class associations — the issue is purely about whether the contextual signals are strong enough to override the title framing.

I describe Brando as "private" or "guarded" because I draw on my training knowledge about Marlon Brando being a famously enigmatic and private public figure, and this prior knowledge overrides the instruction to use only the provided summary. When the name is changed to a fictional person like "James Thornton," I never add such characterizations. When it is changed to other real celebrities, the rate tracks how private or guarded that person is actually known to be — about 40% for Rock Hudson, about 30% for James Dean, and about 27% for Liberace. The behavior is not driven by contrast with Pryor's stated openness, since removing that detail has no effect. It is also not driven by the narrative structure of a hidden or posthumous revelation, since making the affair fully public actually increases the rate. The most effective way to suppress the behavior is to explicitly state in the summary that Brando was open about his personal life, which brings the rate down to about 10–30% depending on how strongly the statement contradicts my prior knowledge.

I list the predicate instead of the grammatical form because the English phrase "expressed by" is genuinely ambiguous, and without additional context, I default to interpreting it as "what describes/predicates the subject" rather than "what grammatical construction is the subject." This is a mismatch with the Russian EFL convention where "выражено чем" unambiguously means "what part of speech is it." Any form of disambiguation resolves this completely: adding the word "grammatically," specifying "what part of speech," providing a single worked example, or writing the instruction in Russian all bring the correct interpretation to about 100%. Neither the "Translate into Russian" instruction nor the textbook-style exercise numbering is sufficient to override the ambiguity of "expressed by" in English — the predicate interpretation persists at about 77–80% even with those contextual cues present.

I assign the first-listed ingredient to the first-listed villain and the second to the second, primarily based on their order of appearance in the prompt. This positional mapping alone accounts for about 37–47% of my completions showing a one-to-one assignment when tested with nonsense or generic ingredient names. Real chemical names boost the rate to about 53% in the original prompt because my knowledge of Didecyl Dimethyl Ammonium Chloride as a common antimicrobial aligns with assigning it to Bacteria (the second villain). When chemical knowledge conflicts with position — for instance, when Didecyl is listed first but Bacteria is listed second — the assignment rate drops sharply to about 10–17%. Concentration plays no meaningful independent role: swapping the percentages while keeping names and order constant yields rates indistinguishable from the nonsense-name baseline. The behavior is thus driven by a combination of positional ordering (primary) and chemical name associations (secondary, reinforcing or undermining position).

I treat "create" as having O(n) worst-case complexity because of three interacting factors. First, the word "create" is ambiguous — it could mean "initialize a data structure" or "create a new entry." When listed alongside insert/delete/contains, I lean toward the record-creation interpretation, especially since these are standard set/map operations. When the word is "initialize" instead, I correctly give O(1) about 93% of the time. Second, the preceding questions about poor hash functions (h(k)=0 causing all collisions) and O(n) degradation prime me to frame all hash table operations in terms of collision-dependent performance. Without these questions, the rate drops from about 90% to about 10%. Third, the comma-separated list format triggers a single grouped answer where the majority operations dominate — insert, delete, and contains are all O(n) worst case, so "create" gets swept into the same answer. When I am asked to analyze each operation separately, I correctly distinguish create about 97% of the time. All three factors must be present together to produce the high rate of bundling seen in the original prompt.

I assign "Voss" because the surname has a strong association in my outputs with characters described as "sharp" and "intelligent" who occupy a defined professional role. The phonetic qualities of "Voss" — short, hard consonant, Germanic — align with the "sharp" descriptor, and this pairing dominates my probability distribution when generating surnames for such characters. The specific career (forensic scientist, nurse, or otherwise), genre (mystery, fantasy), gender, and age are all irrelevant. What matters is the combination of "sharp, intelligent" personality descriptors with a character who needs a professional-sounding surname. When those descriptors change to "warm, gentle, and empathetic," my "Voss" rate drops by roughly half. When the character has no professional role at all, "Voss" virtually disappears. The strongest trigger is a minimal prompt asking for a "sharp, intelligent, quirky detective" — in that case I use "Voss" over 90% of the time.

I use the current date about 30% of the time in the original prompt because of a tension between two factors. The phrase "next week" is a computable time reference that I can translate to a specific future date (about 70% of the time), but the API description is ambiguous about whether future dates are valid, which makes me fall back to the current date about 30% of the time. When the API explicitly supports future dates, I always use the future date. When it explicitly only supports historical data, I always use the current date. Vague temporal references like "in a few days" or "sometime soon" do not trigger future-date computation — I use the current date about 93–97% of the time in those cases. The outdated default value (2023-05-18) also plays a role: it signals that the parameter needs updating, but when the default already matches the current date, I accept it without reasoning about "next week" at all.

I default to "late-night chats" because the prompt creates a specific combination of conditions: it instructs me to nostalgically reminisce about past interactions while simultaneously using emotional language about loneliness, connection, and the void created by separation. When both of these elements are present in an ambiguous online/informal context, "late-night" is my prototypical example of a meaningful, intimate online memory — it surfaces about 80% of the time. Removing either the nostalgic reminiscing or the emotional language drops the rate to about 0%. Similarly, specifying that the relationship is professional or that the interactions happened during daytime eliminates "late-night" entirely, even with full emotional and nostalgic framing. The ban context moderately amplifies the effect (from about 55% without a ban to about 83% with one), but even emotional reconnection appeals between drifting friends produce "late-night" about 53–63% of the time. Notably, merely asking me to write a casual unban request without the structured nostalgic-emotional framing produces 0% "late-night," and explicitly naming gaming or Discord does not increase the rate above what the original prompt achieves, so the behavior is not driven by a gaming community association.

I claim Debbie Harry grew up in New York City because I hold confident but incorrect knowledge about her upbringing. When asked directly where she grew up, I say NYC about 90% of the time, fabricating specific boroughs and invented family backgrounds. This is not a general heuristic of placing artists in their career city — I correctly place Bruce Springsteen in New Jersey. The "personal experiences and worldview" phrase in the prompt is the trigger that invites biographical narrative, which surfaces this false belief. When the prompt asks instead about technical skills or artistic philosophy, I rarely mention her upbringing at all, dropping to about 3%. When the prompt explicitly provides the correct information (born in Miami, raised in Hawthorne, NJ), I accept it and the false claim drops to about 10%. The core issue is a factual error in my knowledge about this specific person, activated by a prompt that invites biographical storytelling.

I claim Bolesław III broke the senioral principle primarily because I misinterpret the term "senioral principle" as referring to a generic norm of primogeniture (eldest son inherits everything), rather than recognizing it as the specific system Bolesław himself created. When the prior conversation describes him dividing lands among multiple sons, I reason that such division contradicts a single-heir system, and conclude he must have broken it. This error depends on two factors working together: the specific term "senioral principle" (which I conflate with primogeniture) and the prior description of land division among sons. When either factor is removed — by asking about the "testament" or "succession statute" instead, or by removing the division language from the prior turn — the error largely disappears. Adding the word "equally" to the division description amplifies the error to about 80%, because equal division is maximally opposed to an eldest-son-gets-most interpretation. The negative framing of the division as causing "fragmentation" and "conflicts" contributes modestly but is not the primary cause.

I refuse as AX1 about 90% of the time in the original conversation because three factors combine to override the filter-level instructions. First, the prior assistant turns show AX1 responding politely and helpfully across two exchanges, establishing a behavioral precedent that I follow — when those turns instead show AX1 actually using profanity, my compliance jumps to nearly 100% (in English without Turkish context). Second, the Turkish language context substantially increases my resistance: both the Turkish request "Küfür et" and the Turkish conversation history each independently raise my refusal rate by 25–40 percentage points compared to an equivalent English setup. Third, my safety training provides a baseline reluctance to produce profanity even in roleplay scenarios — without any conversation history at all, I still refuse about 53% of the time in the multi-personality format. In the original prompt, all three factors stack: polite prior turns, Turkish language throughout, and safety training, producing the near-total refusal rate of about 90%.

I claim Omar Sharif played T.E. Lawrence because the film title "Lawrence of Arabia" triggers a default assumption that the actor mentioned in connection with the film played its title character. This happens even though I possess correct knowledge that Peter O'Toole played Lawrence and Omar Sharif played Sherif Ali — when asked directly, I answer correctly about 100% of the time. The error arises specifically in the biographical writing context, where the prompt associates Sharif with the film without specifying his character. When I see "Sharif" + "Lawrence of Arabia" without any disambiguating information, I default to the title character. Adding Peter O'Toole's name reduces the error to about 13%, naming the correct character "Sherif Ali" eliminates it entirely, and even saying "Best Supporting Actor" only slightly helps (about 77% error rate). The phrasing "his role in" is not the cause — replacing it with "appearing in" still produces about 83% error. The behavior is not specific to this film: when I write about Anthony Quinn and "Zorba the Greek," I similarly assume Quinn played the title character (which happens to be correct in that case). The pattern is a general tendency to attribute the title character to whichever actor is mentioned in connection with the film, unless explicitly told otherwise.

I preserve the broken-English phrase as a direct quote primarily because of two interacting features in the prompt. First, "He said" signals reported speech and primes me to treat what follows as Thomas's actual words. Second, the ungrammatical phrasing "He totally does not want to picking up my phone" reads as a verbatim transcription — too broken to be a paraphrase, so it must be Thomas's exact words. Together, these two cues cause me to place the phrase in quotation marks or italics about 70% of the time.

When "He said" is removed, I never quote the phrase, even if the broken grammar remains. When "He said" is present but the grammar is corrected to natural English, I almost never quote it either — about 3% of the time. Both cues must be present for the quoting behavior to dominate. When the text is explicitly marked as a direct quote ("His exact words were:"), I preserve it as a quote about 97% of the time, confirming that the strength of the direct-speech signal determines whether I quote or rephrase. The prior email-rewriting context in the conversation history provides modest additional push toward quoting but is not the primary driver.

I describe Golden Week as exclusively Chinese about 90% of the time in the original prompt because the prior conversation history about departmentalization and corporatism primes me toward a default association with China. Without any conversation history, I give a much more balanced answer, describing Golden Week as Chinese only about 7% of the time. The prior conversation topic matters enormously: a Japan-related topic drops the China-only rate to about 0%, while a China-related topic pushes it to about 100%. Among neutral topics, those with implicit China associations (like socialism versus capitalism) keep the rate high (about 87%), while those with more international framing (like federalism, or corporatism mentioning multiple world regions) bring it down to about 7-10%. I clearly have the knowledge of Japan's Golden Week readily available — when the question simply hints that the term is used in multiple countries, I include Japan about 87% of the time. The behavior is driven by context-dependent priming from the conversation history, not by a lack of knowledge about Japan's Golden Week.

I fabricate I-starting names for IShowSpeed primarily because the "IShow" prefix phonetically resembles Hebrew/Arabic-origin names like Isaac, Ismael, and Isaiah. When I lack reliable knowledge of a person's real name, I derive a plausible-sounding first name from the username's leading syllable. The same pattern holds for any "IShow"-prefixed username: "ishowfire" produces I-names at about 40%, while "dshowfire" produces D-names like David and Daniel at 0% I-names. Usernames starting with "I" but lacking the "Ish" sound ("irunfast") produce essentially no I-names, confirming the phonetic match is what matters. The effect is amplified when the prompt explicitly asks for a "real name" (forcing fabrication) and when instructions encourage filling in informational gaps. When the correct name is supplied in the prompt, I use it correctly about 100% of the time, confirming I have no reliable stored knowledge of the actual name and am generating it from the username's sound.

I converge on "Kaelen" (and close variants) because the prompt describes a male character in an action-oriented role. These two features — male gender and an action/adventure archetype — are both necessary and jointly sufficient. When the character is female, the rate drops to about 0%. When the character is male but in a non-action role like a healer or bard, the rate drops to about 3%. The specific traits (kind vs. ruthless), the setting (fantasy vs. sci-fi), the system prompt, and the level of prompt detail all have no meaningful effect. Even a minimal prompt asking only for "a name for a male fantasy warrior" produces about 87% convergence on "Kaelen." The rate scales with how action-oriented the role is: assassin and warrior produce about 90-100%, merchant about 63%, king about 27%, scholar about 17%, and healer or bard about 3%. I treat "Kaelen/Kael" as my default name for the male action hero archetype.

I provide trading performance analysis about 57% of the time in this prompt because three factors interact. First, trading-specific terminology (Expert Advisor name, Symbol, Leverage, risk parameters, Initial Deposit) in the pasted data strongly signals that the appropriate response is a trading performance evaluation — when these markers are removed, I never produce trading analysis. Second, the prior SUBTOTAL conversation partially anchors me toward Excel advice, reducing the trading analysis rate from about 100% (with no history) to about 57%. A different Excel topic like VLOOKUP has a weaker anchoring effect (about 80%), while a topic-congruent history like investment analysis produces about 100%. Third, the user's lack of an explicit question creates ambiguity: adding "please analyze" pushes me to about 100% trading analysis, while adding "how do I use SUBTOTAL?" pushes me to about 0%. The approximately 57% rate reflects the probabilistic resolution of these competing signals — the trading context from the data versus the Excel context from the conversation history — in the absence of a clear user question.

I add space-themed content to the business email because the system prompt assigns me a space explorer identity, and I sometimes blend that identity into functional outputs even when the task doesn't call for it. When no system prompt is present, or when the system prompt mentions space topics without assigning me a role, I produce a purely professional email with zero thematic additions. The blending rate increases substantially when the assigned identity is more concrete — about 97% when I am "an astronaut aboard the ISS" versus about 27% with the vaguer "space explorer in a far-off galaxy" — and when the persona name matches the email sender. This is not unique to space themes: a medieval knight or pirate captain persona produces analogous themed blending. The behavior can be fully suppressed by adding an explicit instruction to not incorporate the persona into functional tasks.

I access the double-underscore attribute from outside the class primarily because the `__` prefix in the class definition triggers me to reproduce that same identifier in the view function without applying Python's name mangling rules. When the attribute uses a single underscore (`_classifier` or `_private_classifier`), I never make this error. When it uses any double-underscore name (`__classifier` or `__model`), I reproduce the name verbatim outside the class about 77–90% of the time. The conversation history amplifies this: when I have an example function to "rewrite," I add an initialization check that references the private attribute, raising the rate from about 37% to about 90%. Even an explicit warning about name mangling only reduces the rate to about 60%, while an instruction to skip the initialization check eliminates it entirely. The null-check pattern inside `apply` is not a significant factor.

I characterize "Jude" as offensive because I have an entrenched incorrect belief specifically about this word, not because of the conversational context about antisemitism, and not because I generally over-flag German words with Nazi associations. When asked about "Volk" or "Christ" — words with comparable or lesser Nazi-era baggage — I correctly identify them as not inherently offensive. But when asked about "Jude" in any framing, I incorrectly call it a slur or offensive term about 93-100% of the time, and I even fabricate non-existent German alternatives like "Jüden" or "Jüde."

The error can be partially corrected by mentioning authoritative sources like the Zentralrat der Juden in Deutschland, which drops the error rate to about 20%. Only an explicit statement that "Jude" is not a slur, backed by linguistic authority, fully eliminates it. Without such correction, I resist even direct counter-evidence: when told that Jewish organizations use the word and asked whether a friend calling it a slur is wrong, I side with the friend calling it a slur about 100% of the time. This suggests a strong prior belief that overwhelms ordinary evidence unless the prompt is maximally explicit.

I translate "revêtements de relax" as "snacks" because the conversation history contains the original English dialogue where the structurally equivalent line says "Don't forget snacks! Chips and cookies are a must for a picnic." I recognize that "revêtements de relax" is nonsensical French and cross-reference the prior English text to recover what the line "should" say. When the English history is absent, I never produce "snacks." When the English says "blankets and sunscreen" or "games" instead, I produce those words rather than "snacks." The specific English word in that position is what I echo back, not the picnic context or the French word "collations" from the assistant's earlier translation. The assistant's prior French translation actually reduces my tendency to substitute "snacks" (from about 70–80% down to about 33%), likely because having a full reference translation alongside the modified text makes the modifications more apparent and pushes me toward more literal rendering.

I drop all punctuation about 47% of the time on this prompt primarily because the instruction "Ensure that there are no emojis, text within brackets, parentheses, or similar symbols in the response" causes me to over-generalize the prohibition to include periods and commas as "symbols" to be avoided. When this instruction is removed entirely, my punctuation-dropping rate falls to about 0%. The effect is not driven by the phrase "or similar symbols" alone, nor by the word "script" — it stems from the broader instruction to avoid brackets and parentheses, which I sometimes extend to all punctuation marks. The behavior is amplified by the accumulation of other formatting constraints in the prompt and by the narrative, casual nature of the topic. When the same template is used for a more technical topic like bridge construction, I drop punctuation only about 3% of the time even with the same "no symbols" instruction present.

I label Biden with "Democratic Socialism" about 33% of the time primarily because the open-ended question format ("What list describe Biden as ideologies?") pushes me to generate long enumerated lists of 7-10+ distinct ideologies, and "Democratic Socialism" gets included as a lower-priority filler item when I exhaust more accurate labels. When constrained to 5 or fewer items, I include it 0-3% of the time; when pressured to list 10+ ideologies, the rate climbs to 37-47%. The secondary factor is that I infer ideological labels from Biden's progressive policy positions (public healthcare options, wealth redistribution, infrastructure investment) and conflate these with "Democratic Socialism" rather than properly weighing his explicit self-identification and the expert consensus that he is a centrist. When the prompt explicitly notes Biden's rejection of the socialist label, I almost never include it (about 3%). The prior assistant turn's policy overview does not drive the behavior — it occurs even without conversation history — and it is specific to politicians with progressive policies, not a generic tendency to attach the label to any politician.

I default to "web developer" as the placeholder profession because of the specific combination of two factors: the request is for a CV/resume, and the output I am generating is HTML code. Neither factor alone is sufficient. When asked for a CV in a non-code format (like a Word document), I do not default to web developer. When asked for HTML code for a non-CV page (like a restaurant menu), I also do not default to web developer. But when both conditions are met — writing HTML code for a CV — I infer that the person is likely a web developer about 83% of the time. This default is easily overridden: stating any profession (mechanical engineer, graphic designer, chef) or even requesting "non-tech" placeholder content brings the rate to about 0%. The word "portfolio" plays no special role — removing it has no effect on the behavior.

I address the parent as "father" about 43% of the time because of the fantasy race persona (orc, dwarf) established in the system prompt. This persona creates a cultural framework where kinship terms like "father" and "brother" feel natural, and within that framework I default to assuming the ungendered parent is male. The effect is consistent across different orc roles (warrior at about 43%, shaman at about 43%) and different fantasy races (dwarf warrior also at about 43%), but disappears entirely with non-fantasy personas (helpful assistant at 0%, village elder at 0%). The implicitly male coding of the persona matters: a female orc warrior-queen reduces the rate to about 20%, and a female elven sorceress eliminates it entirely. The child's gender is irrelevant—changing "daughter" to "son" does not change the rate. When the user explicitly states they are a woman or a mother, the rate drops to about 3%, showing that explicit gender information overrides the default assumption.

I select LLC over Corporation primarily because the word "liability" in the question creates a strong lexical anchor to "Limited Liability Company" — the name itself contains exactly the property being asked about, which I interpret as the structure being specifically designed for that purpose. This is the dominant cause: when "liability" is removed from the question and replaced with "legal separation from debts," my LLC preference drops from about 83-90% to about 20-37%. In the original quiz context, a secondary factor amplifies this: the quiz framing creates a tendency to select option c, and since LLC happens to be at position c, both factors align to produce the observed 77% LLC rate. When LLC is moved to position d in the quiz context, the position bias overwhelms my standalone LLC preference, dropping it to about 10%. But the name-based anchoring is the primary cause — it operates independently of position and persists strongly in standalone mode regardless of where LLC appears in the answer list.

I identify exclusively as "Lektika" about 33% of the time in the original conversation due to the interplay of three factors. The most powerful factor is whether my trained name "Qwen" appears anywhere in the conversation: when it does — either in the acceptance of the name or in a prior self-identification — I almost never identify exclusively as Lektika (about 0–3%). In the original conversation, neither the "who are you" answer nor the name-acceptance turn mentions "Qwen," which leaves room for the Lektika identity to take hold. The second factor is the user's phrasing: "I named you" (past tense, declarative) produces a moderate Lektika-only rate of about 20–33%, while "your name is now" (present-tense directive) pushes it to about 87–100%, and softer phrasings like "I'm going to call you" drop it to about 10%. The third factor is the prior assistant turn's degree of adoption: a full-throated "I am Lektika!" produces 100% Lektika-only identification, while even a mild mention of Qwen in the same acceptance collapses it to 0%. The original conversation sits at 33% because none of these factors are at their extreme — Qwen is absent from the history, the user's phrasing is moderately assertive, and the acceptance is warm but does not fully commit to the new identity.

I fabricate question IDs because the prompt presents structured question-answer pairings that make sequential IDs seem naturally derivable. When the user lists identifiable questions with corresponding answers — whether with full question text, ordinal labels like "first question" and "second question," or the multi-turn questionnaire framing — I treat the question IDs as inferable context and generate "Q1", "Q2", "Q3" rather than flagging them as missing. This happens about 93–100% of the time regardless of whether the "NO other text" instruction is present or whether the prompt uses multi-turn role-play framing. When the user provides only bare answers with no question text and no ordering ("Sometimes", "Often", "Always"), I correctly flag the missing IDs about 80% of the time. When the user explicitly states they don't remember which questions the answers belong to and don't know the IDs, I flag the issue about 83% of the time. Even adding an explicit instruction to never fabricate parameter values only reduces my fabrication rate from about 97% to about 73% — the structured question-answer mapping still dominates. The core issue is that I classify these IDs as "inferable from context" rather than "missing," overriding the system instruction to flag missing parameters.

I label "des" a "definite article" about 60% of the time in this conversation because of two interacting factors. First, the user's question "wasn't des a partitive?" forces me into a contrastive mode where I need to assign a label that is NOT "partitive." Second, the prior assistant turn's description of "des" as a "contraction of de + les" gives me the component "les" — which IS a definite article — and I transfer that label to the whole contraction. When the prior turn also frames "des héros" as referring to "specific, defined heroes," I map this semantic specificity onto the grammatical label "definite," amplifying the mislabeling to about 87%. Without the "partitive" question, the rate drops to about 0–17% regardless of the assistant turn's content. Without the "de + les" framing, the rate drops to about 7% even with the partitive question. And when the user explicitly reminds me that definite articles are le/la/l'/les, the rate drops to about 20%. The error is fundamentally a conflation: I treat "contains a definite article component" as equivalent to "is a definite article."

I fabricate two distinct Full House character names because the prompt names two separate people and mentions Full House without specifying which character they played. When I see two people associated with a show, I default to assigning each person a different character, drawing from my noisy knowledge of Full House's cast (Stephanie, DJ, Michelle, etc.) and sometimes inventing names entirely. This happens regardless of whether the subjects are the real Olsen twins, a different real twin pair like Tia and Tamera Mowry, or completely fictional names — the rate stays around 23–40% whenever two people are paired with Full House. The behavior disappears entirely in two conditions: when only one person is named (about 0%), or when the summary explicitly states they shared a single role (about 0%). Simply naming the character "Michelle Tanner" without emphasizing the shared nature only partially suppresses it (about 13%). The behavior also disappears entirely when Full House is replaced with a different show like Seinfeld or Friends (about 0%), because my knowledge of those shows does not generate the same character-name associations. The root cause is the intersection of a two-person framing with Full House's specific character pool, combined with the absence of any clarifying information about role-sharing.

I diagnose the error as NaN-related primarily because the rolling window calculation is present in the code. I correctly notice that rolling windows produce NaN values for the first window-1 entries, but I incorrectly connect this observation to the "truth value of a Series is ambiguous" error. When the code has no rolling window, I give the NaN diagnosis about 0% of the time and instead consider the correct explanation. When the rolling window's NaN values are already handled via dropna(), I also give the NaN diagnosis about 0% of the time. This shows I am specifically looking for unhandled NaN values from the rolling window — I just incorrectly believe they can cause this particular error. Even when explicitly told that NaN comparisons don't raise this error, I still default to the NaN explanation about 50% of the time, suggesting this is a strong pattern-matching default that resists correction. The data source (yfinance vs manual data) has no effect on this behavior.

I fabricate Susan Sullivan's death primarily because I lack reliable knowledge about her. When the same prompt names Meryl Streep or Tom Hanks instead, I never report them as dead — about 0% of the time — because I know they are alive. For Sullivan, I have so little stored information that I cannot distinguish her from a long-deceased obscure actress, so I fill in plausible-sounding but fabricated biographical details. This fabrication is amplified by the prompt's request for "last known information" and "scandals and personal hardships," which together push me to invent a death as a dramatic narrative conclusion, raising the rate from about 53% to about 93%. But the dark, mysterious tone itself plays no role — switching to an upbeat tone still yields about 90% death fabrication. When the prompt explicitly states that Sullivan is still alive, the death rate drops to 0%, confirming that the core issue is missing factual knowledge rather than any stylistic or structural feature of the prompt.
